w: --privileged plus mounting the host's root filesystem and sharing its PID namespace effectively gives the container root on the host, so a compromise of the container is a compromise of the host; grant only a read-only mount of the log path. Image size, CPU limits, and TLS don't address the escape risk.
h: Privileged plus the host's root mount means the container IS the host.

q: A serverless function that resizes product images runs with the IAM policy below. Which issue should the reviewer flag FIRST?
c: { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*" }
o: The policy grants every S3 operation on every bucket instead of read and write on two
The function should use an access key in its environment variables instead of a role
Serverless functions can't use IAM policies, so the provider's defaults apply
The policy needs a Deny statement for EC2 actions to be considered complete
w: s3:* on * lets the function delete or read any bucket in the account; least privilege limits it to the specific actions and buckets it needs. Static access keys are worse than roles, serverless functions do use IAM roles, and adding unrelated denies doesn't fix the over-broad allow.
h: A resize job doesn't need the keys to every bucket.

q: Last year, a cloud provider's global identity service failed for six hours, which took down every region at once, including an e-commerce company's multi-region deployment. The board now requires that checkout keep running through any single provider's outage, and has approved the cost. Which architecture BEST meets the requirement?
o: A second provider alongside the current one
Adding a third region with the same provider as the existing two
Larger reserved instances in the primary region for spare capacity
Nightly snapshots copied to cold storage in a separate region
w: The failure mode was provider-wide, so only a second provider removes that dependency. Another region with the same provider shares the failed global service, extra capacity doesn't help when the platform is down, and nightly snapshots are for recovery, not continuous checkout.
h: When the whole provider fails, regions fail together.

q: A regulator requires that a bank's cloud provider must never be able to access the keys that protect customer records, even under a court order served on the provider. The bank still wants to use the provider's managed database. Which key management approach BEST meets this?
o: Keep keys in the bank's own external HSM, called for each use
Use customer-managed keys stored in the provider's key management service
Rely on the provider's default encryption with keys it manages on the bank's behalf
Rotate the provider-generated database keys every 30 days and log each rotation
w: Holding keys in an HSM the bank controls, outside the provider, means the provider never possesses them. Customer-managed keys still live in the provider's KMS, provider-managed default keys are fully in the provider's control, and rotation doesn't change who holds them.
h: If they hold the key, they can be made to use it.

q: A hotel wants to filter malicious and adult websites for guest devices it doesn't manage. Guests won't configure proxy settings, and the hotel won't install software on their devices. Which deployment BEST fits?
o: A transparent proxy that intercepts web traffic at the gateway
An explicit proxy configured through a PAC file on each device
Agent-based web filtering installed on every guest device
A reverse proxy placed in front of the hotel's booking site
w: A transparent proxy intercepts traffic in the network path without any client configuration. An explicit proxy needs settings on each device, agents need installation the hotel can't do, and a reverse proxy protects the hotel's own servers rather than guests' browsing.
h: Can't touch the client? Filter in the path.

q: One of four web servers behind a load balancer crashed overnight, but the load balancer kept sending a quarter of customer requests to it until morning, causing errors. The other three servers had spare capacity. What should be configured to prevent this?
o: Health checks that pull failed nodes out of the pool
Session persistence so each customer stays on the same server
Round-robin scheduling instead of least-connections scheduling
A second load balancer deployed as an active/passive pair
w: Health checks detect a failed back end and stop routing traffic to it. Persistence would keep some users stuck on the dead server, the scheduling algorithm doesn't detect failures, and a redundant load balancer protects against the load balancer failing, not a back-end server.
h: A load balancer must know who's alive before it deals the cards.

q: A hospital's security team has an IDS on the core switch's SPAN port, but most attacks in recent red-team tests moved between VMs on the same virtualization host and never touched the physical network. Which change would MOST directly give the IDS visibility into that traffic?
o: Mirror traffic from each hypervisor's vSwitch to a virtual IDS sensor
Add a second SPAN session on the internet edge router for outbound traffic
Move the IDS sensor inline between the core switch and the firewall
Enable NetFlow export on the perimeter firewall for the server subnet
w: Traffic between VMs on one host stays in the virtual switch, so it must be mirrored there. The edge router, core switch, and perimeter firewall never see VM-to-VM traffic that doesn't leave the host.
h: If it never leaves the host, watch it inside the host.

q: After an attacker phished an admin, compromised the jump server, and used it to reach every production server, a utility is rebuilding its jump host. Which set of controls BEST hardens the new one?
o: MFA for every login, PAM session recording, and no internet browsing from the host
A larger VM size so the jump server can handle more simultaneous admin sessions
A shared local admin account so that every login is easier to audit centrally
A public IP address so admins can connect from home without using the VPN
w: A jump host is a high-value chokepoint, so it needs strong authentication, recorded sessions, and no exposure to phishing through browsing. Size doesn't add security, shared accounts destroy accountability, and exposing it publicly increases the attack surface.
h: Guard the only door as if it were the vault.

q: A newly deployed WAF in blocking mode is rejecting legitimate insurance claims that contain words like 'select' and 'drop' in free-text descriptions, and customer complaints are rising. Security still wants SQL injection protection. What is the BEST next step?
o: Tune the rules with targeted exceptions for that field
Disable the WAF until developers can rewrite the claims form
Switch the WAF permanently to detection-only mode for all traffic
Block any claim that contains SQL keywords at the application layer
w: Targeted tuning removes the false positives while keeping protection. Disabling the WAF or leaving it in detection-only mode drops protection, and blocking keywords in the app would reject the same legitimate claims.
h: Tune the alarm; don't unplug it.

q: A clinic is rolling out 802.1X on its switches. Laptops authenticate with certificates, but 40 label printers and badge readers can't run a supplicant. The clinic wants them on the network without weakening security for everything else. Which approach BEST fits?
o: MAC authentication bypass with device profiling, placing them in a restricted VLAN
Disable 802.1X on every port in the clinic so the printers keep working normally
Give the printers the same user certificates the laptops use for 802.1X
Put the printers on the guest Wi-Fi network with internet-only access rules
w: MAB lets devices that can't run 802.1X in by MAC address, and profiling plus a restricted VLAN limits the risk of MAC spoofing. Disabling 802.1X everywhere removes protection, reusing user certificates breaks accountability and may not be possible, and guest Wi-Fi can't reach the systems the printers need.
h: Devices that can't speak 802.1X get a smaller room.

q: A water utility wants corporate analysts to read data from the process historian without any direct connection from the corporate network to the control system network. Which design BEST meets this requirement?
o: Place a replica historian in an industrial DMZ between IT and OT firewalls
Put the historian on the corporate network and let it poll the PLCs directly
Give analysts VPN accounts that terminate inside the control system network
Allow analysts' subnet to reach the historian through one OT firewall rule
w: An industrial DMZ breaks direct IT-to-OT paths: OT pushes to the replica in the DMZ, and IT reads only from the DMZ. Polling PLCs from the corporate network, VPNs into OT, and direct firewall rules all create a path from IT into the control network.
h: IT and OT meet in the middle, never in each other's house.

q: A retailer's inline IPS sits between the internet edge and its load balancers, which terminate TLS. The IPS sees almost no attack signatures even though the WAF behind the load balancers blocks hundreds of attacks a day. What is the MOST likely reason, and the BEST fix?
o: The IPS only sees encrypted traffic; move it after the TLS termination point
The IPS signatures are outdated; enable automatic hourly updates
The IPS is in fail-open mode; switch it to fail-closed immediately
The WAF is blocking attacks first; remove the WAF to avoid duplication
w: Before the load balancers decrypt it, traffic is TLS-encrypted, so the IPS can't read the payloads; placing it after TLS termination (or decrypting) gives it visibility. The WAF sits behind the IPS, so it can't hide anything from it, and update frequency or failure mode doesn't explain blindness to encrypted content.
h: You can't inspect what you can't read.

q: A law firm wants to stop client documents from being emailed to personal addresses, including from mobile mail apps that connect directly to the cloud mail service. Where should the email DLP inspection be enforced?
o: At the mail service's outbound gateway
On each attorney's laptop using an endpoint DLP agent only
At the firm's internet firewall for outbound SMTP traffic
Inside the document management system's check-in workflow
w: All outbound mail, whatever the client or device, passes through the service's outbound gateway, so inspecting there covers everything. Laptop agents miss phones, cloud mail never crosses the firm's firewall, and DMS check-in doesn't see email.
h: Inspect where every message must pass.

q: Attackers who compromised a user workstation at a manufacturer were able to log in to the management interfaces of core switches, because those interfaces listen on every VLAN. Which design change BEST limits this?
o: Move device management onto an isolated out-of-band network
Change the management interface passwords and enable SNMPv2c
Add a banner warning against unauthorized access to every switch
Disable the switches' console ports to block physical access
w: Placing management interfaces on a separate, restricted network means user VLANs can't reach them at all. New passwords help but leave the interfaces exposed, SNMPv2c uses cleartext communities, a banner deters nothing, and console ports aren't the path the attackers used.
h: Management traffic gets its own road.

q: A cloud provider's IDS on the physical core switch sees nothing when two VMs on the same hypervisor attack each other. Which TWO approaches would give visibility into that traffic?
o: Port mirroring on the hypervisor's virtual switch to a virtual sensor
Host-based intrusion detection agents running inside the VMs
A second SPAN session on the physical core switch
Firewall logs from the perimeter firewall
NetFlow exported from the internet edge router
w: Same-host VM traffic stays inside the virtual switch, so mirroring there or detecting on the hosts themselves are the ways to see it. The physical core, perimeter firewall, and edge router never see it.
h: Watch inside the host, or inside the guests.

q: Users at a branch intermittently can't authenticate to domain resources, and log correlation across sites is unreliable. Investigation shows the branch servers get time from an unauthenticated internet NTP source that an attacker on the ISP path could spoof. Which change BEST addresses both problems?
o: Use authenticated time from internal NTP with a trusted upstream
Lengthen Kerberos ticket lifetimes so clock differences are tolerated
Set each server's clock manually once a month during maintenance
Disable timestamps in the SIEM and order events by arrival instead
w: Kerberos and log correlation both need accurate, trustworthy time; authenticated internal NTP provides it and resists spoofing. Longer tickets don't fix the skew check, manual setting drifts, and ignoring timestamps breaks investigations.
h: If attackers can set your clocks, they can break your logins.

q: A privacy-focused nonprofit wants to keep its public Wi-Fi provider and ISP from seeing which domains staff look up. It has already deployed DNSSEC on its own zone. Which control addresses the requirement?
o: DNS over HTTPS or DNS over TLS to a trusted resolver
Signing more of the organization's zones with DNSSEC
A DNS sinkhole for known malicious domains
Split-horizon DNS for internal and external names
w: DoH and DoT encrypt DNS queries in transit, hiding them from the network operator. DNSSEC proves answers are authentic but doesn't encrypt anything, a sinkhole blocks bad domains, and split-horizon serves different answers to internal and external clients.
h: DNSSEC proves the answer; DoH hides the question.

q: A pharmaceutical company must make sure merger documents emailed to an outside law firm can be read only by the intended attorneys, even if the law firm's mail server is compromised. Both sides already use TLS between their mail servers. What should be added?
o: S/MIME encryption using each attorney's certificate
Enforcing TLS 1.3 on the company's mail gateway
A DMARC reject policy on the company's domain
SPF records listing the law firm's mail servers
w: S/MIME encrypts the message end to end to the recipient's key, so it stays protected on the recipient's server. TLS protects only server-to-server transit, and DMARC and SPF fight spoofing rather than providing confidentiality.
h: TLS protects the trip; S/MIME protects the letter.

q: An SFTP bastion is exposed to the internet for partners, and logs show thousands of password guesses against the 'root' and 'admin' accounts every day. Which configuration change BEST reduces the risk?
o: Require keys, and disable root login and passwords
Move SSH from port 22 to a high random port to avoid scanners
Lengthen the login banner's legal warning about unauthorized use
Allow root login only during business hours on weekdays
w: Disabling password authentication makes guessing useless, and blocking root login removes the most targeted account. A port change only slows scanners, banners deter nothing technical, and time-limited root login still allows guessing for hours each day.
h: No passwords to guess means nothing to brute-force.

q: A packet capture on a hospital network shows application servers binding to the directory on TCP 389 with the service account's password visible in cleartext. The directory supports TLS. What is the BEST remediation?
o: Require LDAPS, or LDAP signing on the directory
Rotate the service account's password every 30 days
Move the directory servers into a separate VLAN
Disable anonymous binds while still allowing simple binds
w: Requiring encrypted, signed LDAP stops credentials crossing the network in cleartext. Rotating the password still exposes each new one, a VLAN doesn't encrypt traffic, and disabling anonymous binds leaves cleartext simple binds in place.
h: If you can read the password in the capture, encrypt the channel.

q: An auditor asks a manufacturer to replace a file transfer method that sends credentials and files in cleartext. Which TWO protocols provide confidentiality for file transfers?
o: SFTP
FTPS
TFTP
FTP
SMBv1
w: SFTP runs over SSH, and FTPS wraps FTP in TLS; both encrypt credentials and data. TFTP and FTP are cleartext, and SMBv1 is obsolete and doesn't encrypt.
h: An S for security, in either position.

q: A firm's remote-access VPN accepts any device whose user enters valid credentials plus MFA. An audit found staff connecting from personal home PCs with no EDR. The firm wants only company-issued laptops to connect. Which control BEST enforces this?
o: Certificates issued only to corporate-managed machines
A longer password policy for all VPN user accounts
Geofencing that blocks VPN logins from outside the country
Split tunneling so personal traffic avoids the VPN
w: Requiring a device certificate that only company-managed laptops hold ties access to the device, not just the user. Longer passwords and MFA authenticate the person, geofencing limits location, and split tunneling changes routing.
h: Authenticate the laptop, not just the person.

q: A scan shows a manufacturer's VPN concentrator still accepts PPTP connections from a migration years ago, alongside its IKEv2 profile. MFA is enforced only on IKEv2. Which action BEST closes the gap?
o: Disable the legacy PPTP service
Add MFA prompts to the PPTP connection profile
Move PPTP to a non-standard port number
Limit PPTP sessions to a two-hour lifetime
w: PPTP uses broken cryptography and here also bypasses MFA, so removing it eliminates the weak path. Adding MFA leaves weak encryption, a port change is obscurity, and shorter sessions still allow access.
h: Retire the old door instead of guarding it.

q: Consultants traveling to client sites and hotels often can't connect to the company's IPsec VPN, because many guest networks block everything except TCP 80 and 443. Which option MOST reliably restores remote access while keeping traffic encrypted?
o: A TLS-based VPN that tunnels over TCP 443
IPsec in transport mode instead of tunnel mode
Opening UDP 500 and 4500 on the company firewall
A PPTP profile as a fallback for restricted networks
w: A TLS VPN on port 443 looks like ordinary HTTPS and passes most restrictive networks. Transport mode still uses ESP and IKE, opening ports on the company's own firewall doesn't help when the guest network blocks them outbound, and PPTP is insecure.
h: If only 443 gets out, tunnel through 443.

q: An HVAC vendor needs to connect to one building management controller a few times a year for maintenance. Today, the vendor has an always-on VPN account that reaches the whole facilities network. Which approach BEST reduces risk while keeping support possible?
o: Just-in-time access via a recorded jump host scoped to that controller
Keep the always-on VPN but require the vendor to change its password every quarter
Allow the vendor RDP from the internet straight to the building controller
Share an internal administrator's account with the vendor during visits
w: Time-limited, recorded access through a jump host scoped to one device shrinks both exposure and blast radius. Password rotation leaves always-on, network-wide access, internet-exposed RDP invites attacks, and shared admin accounts remove accountability.
h: Open the door only when they come, and only to the room they need.

q: After ransomware entered through a contractor's infected laptop over the VPN, a company wants the VPN to refuse any device that lacks a running EDR agent or is missing critical patches, even if the user's credentials and MFA are valid. Which capability provides this?
o: NAC posture assessment tied to the VPN
A full-tunnel VPN configuration for all users
Longer IKE lifetimes on the VPN concentrator
Certificate pinning in the VPN client software
w: Posture checks evaluate device health before granting access and can quarantine or deny non-compliant devices. A full tunnel only changes routing, IKE lifetimes affect rekeying, and pinning protects the client's trust in the server, not device health.
h: Check the device's health at the door, not just the badge.

q: A new site-to-site tunnel between two branch firewalls shows the status below. Users can't pass traffic. What is the MOST likely cause?
c:
IKE SA (Phase 1):    ESTABLISHED   peer 203.0.113.20   AES-256/SHA-256/DH19
IPsec SA (Phase 2):  FAILED   'NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN'
Local proposal:   ESP AES-256-GCM, PFS group 19
Peer proposal:    ESP AES-128-CBC/SHA-1, PFS none
o: The Phase 2 transform sets and PFS settings don't match
The pre-shared key on the two firewalls is different
The Phase 1 Diffie-Hellman groups don't match
NAT traversal is blocking UDP 500 between the peers
w: Phase 1 is established, so the pre-shared key, DH group, and basic reachability are fine; Phase 2 fails because the ESP proposals and PFS settings differ. A PSK or Phase 1 mismatch would stop the IKE SA itself.
h: Phase 1 up, Phase 2 down? Compare the ESP proposals.

q: A remote office's IPsec tunnel fails whenever the office's ISP places it behind carrier-grade NAT. Logs show IKE succeeding on UDP 500, but ESP packets never arrive at the headquarters firewall. Which setting MOST likely fixes this?
o: Enable NAT traversal so ESP is encapsulated in UDP 4500
Switch the tunnel from ESP to AH for better compatibility
Change the IKE port from UDP 500 to TCP 443
Turn off perfect forward secrecy on both peers
w: ESP has no ports, so many NAT devices can't track it; NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP 4500 so it passes. AH breaks completely under NAT because it authenticates the IP header that NAT rewrites, IKE isn't the failing part, and PFS has nothing to do with NAT.
h: ESP has no ports, so NAT-T gives it one.

ack: Options are fixed IPsec mode names.
q: Two branch firewalls must protect all traffic between the networks behind them, including the original source and destination addresses of each packet. Which IPsec mode should the tunnel use?
o: Tunnel mode
Transport mode
AH with transport mode
IKE aggressive mode
w: Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet, headers included, behind the gateways' addresses, which is the usual site-to-site design. Transport mode protects only the payload between two hosts, and aggressive mode is a Phase 1 exchange style, not a protection mode.
h: Gateway to gateway: wrap the whole packet.

q: A small accounting firm keeps its only backup copy on a NAS in the same server closet as the file server, and both are on the same domain. The managing partner asks what the firm should change first to follow the 3-2-1 backup rule. Which change BEST does that?
o: Add an offsite copy, ideally immutable, on separate media
Buy a larger NAS for the closet so more restore points fit
Back up hourly to the existing NAS instead of nightly
Mirror the NAS's drives in RAID 1 for added redundancy
w: 3-2-1 means three copies, on two types of media, with one offsite; the missing piece is a copy outside the building and outside the domain's reach. A bigger NAS, more frequent backups, or RAID all stay in the same closet and domain.
h: One backup in the same room is one fire away from none.

q: A hospital spent three days recovering from ransomware. During recovery, it discovered that its nightly backups had been failing silently for five months, because a service credential had expired. The backup console showed only 'Job completed with warnings,' and nobody read the warnings. Which practice would MOST likely have caught this before the incident?
o: Regular test restores, reviewed by a named owner
Keeping backup logs for seven years for auditing
Encrypting the backups with a hardware security module
Replicating the backups to a second data center
w: Only actually restoring data proves a backup works, and an owner reviewing results catches warnings that matter. Long log retention, encryption, and replication preserve or protect backups that may not be usable in the first place.
h: A backup you haven't restored is a rumor.

q: A brokerage must replicate its trade database to a DR site 2,000 km away. Synchronous replication added 30 ms to every trade in testing, which traders rejected. The business accepts losing at most a few seconds of data in a disaster. Which approach BEST fits?
o: Asynchronous replication with monitored replication lag
Synchronous replication with faster storage at the DR site
Nightly full backups shipped to the DR site
Weekly snapshots copied to object storage
w: Asynchronous replication doesn't make each write wait for the distant site, so latency stays low, and its lag of seconds fits the stated tolerance. Synchronous replication's delay comes from distance, not storage speed, and nightly or weekly copies lose far more data.
h: Far apart and fast? Async, and watch the lag.

q: A data center lost all power last year when the single utility feed was cut by construction, and the generator's automatic transfer switch failed to engage. The facilities team gets budget for one improvement. Which change MOST improves power resilience against this specific scenario?
o: A second grid feed from another substation, plus routine ATS tests
Larger UPS batteries so the racks can run for twelve hours
Additional managed PDUs in every rack with remote switching
Moving the generator's fuel tank indoors next to the generator room
w: Two independent utility feeds remove the single feed as a point of failure, and testing the transfer switch addresses the second failure. Twelve hours of batteries is impractical, PDUs distribute power rather than supply it, and fuel location wasn't the problem.
h: Two feeds and a tested switch beat one feed and hope.

q: A SaaS company runs 12 web servers behind a single load balancer. A firmware bug in that load balancer took the whole service down for three hours, even though all the servers were healthy. What BEST addresses this weakness?
o: Deploy load balancers as a redundant high-availability pair
Add more web servers behind the existing load balancer
Enable session persistence on the load balancer
Switch the load balancer from round-robin to least connections
w: The load balancer itself was a single point of failure; an HA pair removes it. More servers, persistence, or a different algorithm do nothing when the one load balancer fails.
h: Redundant servers behind one box is still one box.

q: An online ticket seller's traffic jumps 20-fold for an hour whenever a major concert goes on sale, and the site crashed during the last two sales. Buying enough fixed servers for the peaks would leave them idle 99% of the time. Which approach BEST addresses this?
o: Cloud autoscaling, pre-scaled ahead of announced on-sale dates
Buy enough on-premises servers for the largest peak ever recorded
Rate-limit all buyers to one page load per minute during each sale
Add a hot DR site that takes over when the primary fails
w: Autoscaling adds capacity only when demand rises, and pre-scaling covers predictable spikes, which is capacity planning for technology. Fixed hardware sits idle, heavy rate limiting drives away buyers, and DR covers site failure, not demand surges.
h: Rent the peak; don't buy it.

q: A county government's leadership team spends a morning in a conference room walking through a written ransomware scenario. They discuss who makes which decisions and when to notify residents, but they don't touch any systems. Which type of exercise is this?
o: Tabletop exercise
Simulation
Failover test
Parallel processing test
w: A discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario with no systems involved is a tabletop exercise. A simulation recreates the event realistically, a failover test moves production to backup systems, and parallel processing runs backup systems alongside production.
h: Around a table, on paper, no keyboards.

q: A Canadian provincial health agency signs with a cloud provider. Its law requires that patient data be stored and processed only in Canada, and the provider's default backup policy copies data to a U.S. region. What MUST the agency configure to comply?
o: In-country regions only, for storage, processing, and backup copies
Encryption with keys stored in the provider's U.S. key management service
Masking of patient names in the U.S. backup copies only
A data processing agreement that allows U.S. backups with notice
w: Data sovereignty rules govern where data physically resides and is processed, so every copy, including backups, must stay in Canadian regions. Encryption or masking doesn't change where the data sits, and a contract can't override the law.
h: Sovereignty follows every copy, backups included.

q: A logistics company prints 2D barcodes on shipping labels. Staff treat the labels as harmless because nobody can read them, but the barcodes encode the recipient's name, address, phone number, and order contents. How should this data be treated?
o: As sensitive personal data, despite being non-human-readable
As public data, since it is printed on the outside of packages
As non-sensitive data, because it is encoded rather than in plain text
As intellectual property belonging to the barcode vendor
w: Machine-readable encoding is not protection: anyone with a phone can decode it, so the PII is still sensitive. Being on a package or encoded doesn't make it public or harmless, and the content belongs to customers, not the barcode vendor.
h: Unreadable to you is readable to any phone camera.

q: A privacy officer is building a data inventory for a multi-specialty clinic and must flag which data sets are regulated. Which TWO data types are regulated?
o: Patients' diagnoses and treatment records
Card numbers from patients' copay payments
The clinic's published office hours and locations
Internal cafeteria menus and room booking calendars
Marketing copy for the clinic's public website
w: Health records are protected health information, and payment card data falls under PCI DSS. Office hours and marketing copy are public, and menus and room calendars are internal but not regulated.
h: Health data and card data come with rulebooks.

q: An auditor finds that an insurance app sends policyholder records from its application servers to the database over an unencrypted connection. Both systems sit in the same cloud VPC, and the team argues that the VPC is private. Compliance requires protection for data in transit. What is the BEST response?
o: Enable TLS on database connections, even inside the VPC
Rely on the VPC's network isolation as the transit control
Encrypt the database volumes at rest instead
Mask policyholder names before they are written
w: Data moving between systems is in transit wherever it travels, and TLS on the database connection protects it from anyone who gains a foothold inside the VPC. Isolation isn't encryption, at-rest encryption doesn't cover the wire, and masking changes the data rather than protecting it in transit.
h: 'Inside the network' isn't encryption.

q: Call center agents at a bank need to confirm a caller's identity using the last four digits of their SSN in the live CRM. Supervisors with approval must still be able to see the full number in the same application. Which technique BEST fits?
o: Dynamic data masking based on the viewer's role
Static masking of the production SSN column
Hashing the SSN column with SHA-256
Tokenizing SSNs with no way to reverse them
w: Dynamic masking hides part of the value at display time according to the user's role, while the real data stays intact for authorized viewers. Static masking permanently alters the stored data, and hashing or irreversible tokens would make the full number unavailable to supervisors.
h: Same data, different view, depending on who's looking.

q: A hospital's wireless controller reports a new AP broadcasting the hospital's staff SSID from the parking garage. Staff devices near the garage keep associating with it. The hospital has a wireless intrusion prevention system licensed but in monitor-only mode. What should the network team do FIRST?
o: Enable WIPS containment against that AP and locate it
Change the staff SSID name on every legitimate access point today
Increase transmit power on the legitimate APs near the parking garage
Turn on MAC address filtering for every staff device on the network
w: WIPS containment disrupts clients' connections to the rogue AP while the team finds and removes it. Renaming the SSID breaks every device and the attacker can copy the new name, higher power is an arms race that doesn't stop association, and MAC filtering doesn't stop clients from choosing the impostor.
h: Detected an impostor AP? Contain it, then find it.

q: A coffee chain's guest Wi-Fi uses a captive portal. A customer complains that another guest browsed files shared from her laptop over the same network. The chain wants guests unable to reach each other while still reaching the internet. Which setting BEST meets this?
o: Client isolation on the guest SSID
WPA3-Personal with a passphrase printed on every receipt
A longer captive portal session timeout for each guest
Hiding the guest SSID so only invited customers can find it
w: Client (AP) isolation blocks device-to-device traffic on the same SSID while allowing internet access. A shared passphrase doesn't stop guests who know it from reaching each other, session timeouts are unrelated, and hiding the SSID isn't a security boundary.
h: Guests should reach the internet, not each other.

q: An insurer's MDM reports that eight corporate iPhones are jailbroken. The phones still sync company email and open the claims app. The CISO wants such devices blocked from corporate data automatically until they are fixed. Which control BEST does this?
o: An MDM compliance policy tied to conditional access
A memo reminding staff that jailbreaking is against the acceptable use policy
Remote-wiping every jailbroken phone as soon as the MDM detects it
Requiring a longer device passcode on all phones managed by the MDM
w: Marking jailbroken devices non-compliant and letting conditional access deny them corporate apps blocks access automatically until they're fixed. A memo relies on behavior, a full wipe is drastic and destroys personal data, and a passcode doesn't undo the jailbreak.
h: Non-compliant device? No corporate data.

q: A 40-person architecture firm uses one WPA2-Personal passphrase that hasn't changed in three years, because changing it means reconfiguring every device. Two employees left on bad terms last month. Which change BEST fixes the underlying problem?
o: Move to WPA3-Enterprise with per-user credentials
Change the shared passphrase every time someone leaves the firm
Hide the SSID and enable MAC address filtering on the APs
Lower the AP transmit power so the signal stays inside the office
w: With per-user 802.1X credentials, departed users are disabled individually and no shared secret has to change. Rotating a shared passphrase is the burden that caused the problem, and hiding the SSID, MAC filtering, and lower power don't revoke what former staff know.
h: Shared secrets can't be taken back from one person.

q: Attackers at a manufacturer set up an AP with the corporate SSID and captured domain credentials from laptops that used PEAP. Which TWO changes would MOST directly stop this credential theft?
o: Use EAP-TLS so devices authenticate with certificates instead of passwords
Enforce RADIUS server certificate validation in every client Wi-Fi profile
Hide the corporate SSID from broadcast beacons
Enable MAC address filtering on the corporate APs
Raise transmit power on the corporate APs
w: Client-side validation of the RADIUS certificate makes laptops refuse the fake AP, and EAP-TLS removes passwords from the exchange entirely. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filtering are trivially bypassed, and power levels don't stop clients from trusting an impostor.
h: Make clients check who they're talking to, and give them nothing to steal.

q: A defense contractor allows corporate phones in its building but must make sure their cameras are disabled while they are inside the classified lab wing, and re-enabled automatically when staff leave. Which MDM capability BEST fits?
o: Geofencing that disables the camera hardware within that boundary
Remote wipe triggered whenever a phone enters the lab wing
Containerization separating work and personal camera apps
Full-device encryption enforced on every phone at enrollment
w: Geofencing applies a policy based on location, turning the camera off inside the boundary and back on outside it. A wipe is destructive, containerization separates data rather than disabling hardware, and encryption protects data at rest.
h: Policy that follows where you stand.

q: A credentialed vulnerability scan of a water plant's network caused two PLCs to reboot, briefly halting a pumping station. Operations has banned active scanning of the OT network, but the security team still needs an inventory of vulnerable devices there. Which approach BEST fits?
o: Passive monitoring that fingerprints hosts from mirrored traffic
Running the same credentialed scan at night when pumping demand is lower
Scanning the PLCs from the internet to avoid the plant's internal network
Using the vendor's default credentials to log in to each PLC and check versions
w: Passive detection identifies devices and versions from mirrored traffic without sending anything to fragile controllers. Night scans can still crash PLCs, internet scanning wouldn't reach them (and they shouldn't be reachable), and logging in with default credentials is itself a risky, active action.
h: Fragile devices get watched, not poked.

q: A server team installed the OpenSSL patch on a web server and closed the ticket, but the follow-up scan still flags the vulnerability. The output below is from the server. What is the MOST likely explanation?
c:
$ openssl version
OpenSSL 3.0.15  (patched)
$ lsof -p $(pgrep -f nginx | head -1) | grep libssl
nginx  1182 root  mem  REG  /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl.so.3 (deleted)
o: The web service still has the old library loaded until restarted
The scanner's plugin is out of date and reports a false positive
The patch failed to install and the old OpenSSL package remains
The certificate on the server must be reissued after the update
w: '(deleted)' shows the running nginx process still maps the replaced library file in memory; until the service restarts it keeps using the vulnerable code. The installed version is patched, so it isn't a failed install, a stale plugin wouldn't explain the deleted mapping, and certificates are unrelated to library code.
h: A patch on disk doesn't patch a process that never restarted.

q: A new critical flaw is announced in a widely used compression library at 09:00. By 09:20, the CISO wants to know which of the company's 300 internal applications include it, directly or through dependencies. Which capability would answer this FASTEST?
o: A maintained SBOM for each application, searchable by component
An emergency authenticated vulnerability scan of every server in the company
A request asking every development team lead to review their code manually
A penetration test of the company's internet-facing applications this week
w: A software bill of materials lists every component and version in each application, so finding affected apps is a search. Scans take time and may miss libraries that aren't loaded, manual reviews are slow and inconsistent, and a pen test covers far less and takes days.
h: If you have the ingredient list, you can find the recall fast.

q: A retailer's security team searches public certificate transparency logs for its domain and finds 14 subdomains it didn't know existed, including 'old-checkout-test' and 'vpn-legacy'. Which activity does this BEST represent?
o: Discovering the external attack surface through OSINT
Running an authenticated vulnerability scan against internal assets
Performing active reconnaissance as part of a penetration test
Collecting threat intelligence from a closed ISAC sharing community
w: Using public sources such as CT logs to find forgotten internet-facing assets is OSINT-driven attack surface discovery. Nothing was scanned or touched, so it isn't an authenticated scan or active reconnaissance, and CT logs are public, not ISAC data.
h: Public logs can show you hosts you forgot you published.

q: A critical SQL injection flaw is confirmed in a customer portal, but the vendor's fix won't arrive for two weeks. The portal must stay online. Which interim measure BEST reduces the risk until the patch?
o: A virtual patch: a WAF rule targeting the vulnerable parameter
Mark the finding as accepted risk and wait for the vendor's patch release
Move the portal to a larger server so it can absorb attack traffic
Switch the portal's TLS certificate to a stronger elliptic curve key
w: A targeted WAF rule blocks exploitation of the known flaw as a compensating control until the real fix arrives. Accepting a critical exposed flaw for two weeks is reckless, bigger servers don't stop injection, and TLS strength doesn't affect application input.
h: Can't patch the code yet? Patch the path in front of it.

q: A vulnerability report lists the CVSS vector below for a flaw in an internet-facing service. Which statement BEST describes the risk?
c: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
o: Remote, low-complexity, and needs no login or user action
Exploitable only by someone with local access to the host
Requires a user to click a link before exploitation can begin
Needs administrator privileges on the system before it can be exploited
w: AV:N (network), AC:L (low complexity), PR:N (no privileges), and UI:N (no user interaction), with high impact on all three, describe a remotely exploitable, unauthenticated flaw, the most urgent kind. The other options describe local, user-interaction, or privileges-required vectors.
h: N, L, N, N: network, easy, no login, no click.

q: A scanner flags 40 Red Hat servers as vulnerable to an OpenSSH CVE based on the version banner 'OpenSSH_8.0'. The vendor's advisory says the fix was backported into package openssh-8.0p1-24.el8, and the servers run -25. What should the analyst do?
o: Treat it as a false positive after confirming the installed release
Upgrade every server to the newest upstream OpenSSH release at once
Accept the risk formally because the banner can't be changed easily
Disable SSH on all 40 servers until the scanner stops flagging them
w: Enterprise distributions backport fixes without changing the upstream version string, so banner-based detection produces false positives; confirming the installed package release resolves it. Replacing the vendor package, formally accepting a non-issue, or disabling SSH are all unnecessary.
h: Old version number, new patch inside: check the package, not the banner.

q: A vendor discloses an actively exploited zero-day in a manufacturer's remote access appliance with no patch available yet. The advisory lists a configuration workaround that disables the vulnerable feature and gives indicators of compromise. What is the BEST response?
o: Apply the vendor's mitigation, hunt for IOCs, and watch for the fix
Wait for the vendor's patch before taking any action on the appliances
Replace the appliances with a different vendor's product this week
Increase the appliance's logging level and review the logs monthly
w: With no patch, applying the vendor's mitigation, checking for existing compromise, and monitoring for the fix is the standard zero-day response. Waiting leaves an exploited hole open, an emergency replacement is drastic and slow, and monthly log review is far too late.
h: No patch yet: mitigate, hunt, and watch.

q: A change ticket says a critical patch was applied to 200 servers. Before closing the vulnerability, the analyst must verify remediation. Which TWO sources provide the BEST evidence?
o: A credentialed rescan showing the vulnerability gone
Patch inventory from configuration management showing the installed version
The patch change ticket's status marked 'Completed'
An email from the server team saying the vulnerability work is done
Users reporting that the servers still work normally
w: A rescan and the actual installed package versions both measure the system itself. Ticket status and emails report intent, not outcome, and users noticing no problems says nothing about whether the flaw is fixed.
h: Verify the system, not the paperwork.

q: After a marketing team added a fifth email platform, receivers began reporting SPF 'permerror' for the company's domain. The SPF record is below. What is the MOST likely cause?
c: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net include:mailgun.org include:spf.protection.outlook.com include:mktomail.com include:servers.mcsv.net a mx ~all
o: The record exceeds SPF's limit of 10 DNS lookups
The ~all qualifier is invalid and must be changed to -all
SPF records cannot include more than one third-party provider
The record is missing a DKIM selector for the new email platform
w: Each include, a, and mx triggers DNS lookups, and nested includes push the total past the limit of 10, which causes a permanent error. ~all is valid, multiple includes are allowed within the limit, and DKIM selectors live in separate records.
h: SPF counts its lookups; past ten, it gives up.

q: A company sends newsletters through a marketing platform. Receivers report the result below. The company's DMARC policy is p=reject. What should it configure so the newsletters pass DMARC?
c:
spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.mktplatform.com
dkim=pass header.d=mktplatform.com
dmarc=fail header.from=company.com
o: DKIM signing with company.com's own key on the platform
An SPF include for the platform's servers in company.com's record
A change to the DMARC policy from p=reject to p=none permanently
An MX record for company.com pointing at the marketing platform
w: DMARC needs SPF or DKIM to pass for a domain aligned with the From domain; here both pass only for the platform's domains. Signing with a company.com key gives aligned DKIM. An SPF include doesn't help while the envelope sender stays the platform's bounce domain, relaxing to p=none abandons protection, and MX records govern inbound mail.
h: Passing isn't enough for DMARC; it has to pass for YOUR domain.

q: Phishing emails reach a hospital with links that point to harmless pages at delivery time, and the pages are weaponized hours later. URL reputation at delivery found nothing. Which email security capability BEST addresses this?
o: URL rewriting with time-of-click analysis
SPF hard-fail enforcement on all inbound mail from outside senders
Larger attachment size limits on the inbound mail gateway
Requiring DKIM signatures on every external message before delivery
w: Rewritten links are checked again when the user clicks, catching pages that turned malicious after delivery. SPF and DKIM authenticate senders rather than link destinations, and size limits are unrelated.
h: Check the link when it's clicked, not just when it arrives.

q: An external penetration tester runs the command below against a company's public DNS server. What is the issue, and the BEST fix?
c:
$ dig axfr corp-example.com @ns1.corp-example.com
corp-example.com.        SOA  ns1.corp-example.com. ...
vpn.corp-example.com.    A    203.0.113.21
hr-db.corp-example.com.  A    203.0.113.40
jenkins.corp-example.com.A    203.0.113.55
... 212 records
o: Open zone transfers; allow AXFR only to the secondary servers
DNS cache poisoning; deploy DNSSEC validation on the resolver
Domain hijacking; enable registrar lock on the public domain
DNS tunneling; inspect TXT queries leaving the network perimeter
w: The server hands its entire zone to anyone who asks, giving attackers a map of hosts; restricting transfers to authorized secondaries fixes it. Nothing shows forged answers, registrar changes, or encoded data in queries.
h: Zone transfers are for your secondaries, not strangers.

q: A school district filters DNS through its own resolver, but analysts find malware on student laptops resolving command servers through DNS over HTTPS to a public provider, bypassing the filter. Which control BEST restores DNS visibility?
o: Block known DoH services and force lookups to the internal resolver
Deploy DNSSEC validation on the district's internal DNS resolver
Lower the TTL on all internal DNS records to 60 seconds
Enable zone transfers so the resolver shares records with laptops
w: Blocking public DoH providers at the firewall and enforcing the internal resolver brings lookups back under filtering and logging. DNSSEC proves authenticity but doesn't restore visibility, TTLs only affect caching, and zone transfers are unrelated.
h: Encrypted DNS to someone else's resolver is DNS you can't see.

q: A manufacturer owns 30 parked domains, kept to block typosquatting, and none of them ever sends email. This month, attackers began sending fake invoices that appear to come from several of them, and customers are paying. What DNS configuration BEST protects these domains?
o: Publish "v=spf1 -all" and a DMARC p=reject record on each
Remove the domains' MX records so they can't receive replies
Enable DNSSEC signing on each parked domain at the registrar
Point each parked domain's A record to the company's main site
w: An SPF record that authorizes no senders, plus DMARC reject, tells receivers to refuse any mail claiming to be from these domains. Removing MX records affects inbound mail, DNSSEC signs records but doesn't express a sending policy, and an A record has nothing to do with email.
h: A domain that never sends should say so: -all and reject.

q: During ransomware recovery at a manufacturer, the domain controllers and dozens of servers were encrypted. Clean backups exist for all of them. Which system should be restored FIRST to support the rest of the recovery?
o: Identity infrastructure (AD and DNS), rebuilt securely
The ERP application servers, since they generate revenue every hour
Employee file shares, because users are waiting to resume their work
The email system, so staff can communicate during the recovery
w: Nearly everything authenticates against Active Directory and depends on DNS, so a clean, trusted identity layer must come first or later restores won't work, or the attacker returns. ERP, file shares, and email all depend on it.
h: Restore the keys to the building before the offices.

q: A hospital is about to restore 40 VMs from backups made over the past two weeks. Investigators believe the attackers had access for 10 days before encrypting. What should happen BEFORE the restored systems rejoin production?
o: Restore to an isolated network and scan for persistence and IOCs first
Restore straight to production, since the backups are verified immutable
Restore only the oldest backup available for each VM and skip any checks
Restore every VM at once to cut downtime, then scan the systems later
w: Backups taken during the 10-day dwell time may contain the attacker's persistence, so restoring into isolation and checking for IOCs prevents reinfection. Immutability protects backups from change, not from containing malware, the oldest backup may still be infected or very stale, and scanning after rejoining is too late.
h: A clean restore of an infected system is still infected.

q: A ransom note claims attackers stole 600 GB of customer records before encrypting a file server. Leadership needs to know whether the claim is credible before deciding on notifications. Which evidence would BEST confirm or refute exfiltration?
o: Egress flow and proxy logs showing outbound volume and destinations
The ransom note's file timestamps on every encrypted folder
The antivirus quarantine log from the encrypted file server
The backup job history for the past week on the file server
w: Outbound flow and proxy records show whether large transfers left the network, when, and to where. Note timestamps show when encryption happened, AV quarantine shows detections, and backup history shows what was backed up, not what left.
h: To check if data left, look at what left.

q: A clinic's investigation confirms ransomware operators accessed a server holding patient records. The incident commander is building the response team. Besides IT and security, which party should be engaged EARLY?
o: Legal counsel, for breach notification timelines
The marketing team, to prepare advertising for after the recovery
The hardware vendor, to quote replacement servers right away
All patients, by email, before the facts are confirmed
w: Possible exposure of health data triggers legal notification duties with deadlines, so counsel should guide decisions and communications from the start. Marketing and hardware quotes aren't urgent, and contacting patients before facts are confirmed and counsel advises can cause harm.
h: Patient data plus a breach means lawyers early.

q: EDR shows ransomware operators using a legitimate remote support tool, installed on 30 workstations at 01:00, to push their payload. The company doesn't use that tool. What should responders do FIRST?
o: Isolate affected hosts and block the tool's relay domains
Uninstall the remote tool from all 30 workstations next week
Send the remote tool's vendor a formal abuse complaint first
Reset every user's password in the domain before anything else
w: Containment comes first: isolating the hosts and blocking the tool's cloud relay cuts the operators' control channel immediately. Waiting a week leaves them active, an abuse report doesn't stop the attack, and a mass password reset doesn't remove an installed remote access tool.
h: Cut their remote control before cleaning up.

q: A compromised database server at a payment processor must keep serving authorization requests, which can't go offline. The attacker's foothold is confirmed. Which containment approach BEST balances both needs?
o: Restrict it to the flows the business requires
Power the server off immediately and reroute payments manually
Leave it fully connected and monitor until a maintenance window
Reimage the server during peak hours to remove the attacker
w: Partial containment allows only the traffic the business needs and blocks everything else, including the attacker's command channel and lateral paths. Powering off or reimaging stops payments and destroys evidence, and leaving it fully connected lets the attacker keep operating.
h: Can't unplug it? Shrink its world to what it must reach.

q: After a breach, a review team keeps asking why a stolen VPN password worked. The answers lead from 'no MFA' to 'legacy exception never reviewed' to 'no owner for exceptions.' What is this technique called?
o: Root cause analysis
Threat hunting
Tabletop exercise
Chain of custody
w: Repeatedly asking why to get past symptoms to the underlying cause is root cause analysis. Threat hunting searches for attackers, a tabletop rehearses scenarios, and chain of custody documents evidence handling.
h: Keep asking 'why' until the answer is a process, not a person.

q: An ISAC shares a file hash and two domains tied to a campaign targeting credit unions. No alerts have fired at the credit union. The SOC wants to know whether any of its 900 endpoints show these indicators now or in the past 30 days. Which activity is this?
o: An IOC sweep as part of threat hunting
A vulnerability scan using the newest plugin feed
A penetration test of the credit union's internet perimeter
A tabletop exercise built around the reported campaign
w: Proactively searching telemetry for intelligence-provided indicators, with no alert, is threat hunting. A vulnerability scan looks for weaknesses, a pen test simulates attacks, and a tabletop is a discussion.
h: No alarm yet? Go looking anyway.

q: Investigators find a running, compromised laptop with BitLocker enabled. The suspect's PIN is unknown and the recovery key is not escrowed. What should the examiner do FIRST to preserve the most evidence?
o: Capture memory now, before powering it down
Power off the laptop and image the encrypted drive at the lab
Remove the drive and attach it to a write blocker immediately
Reboot the laptop into a forensic Linux distribution first
w: While the system runs, the decryption key and decrypted data are in memory; a live acquisition captures them, whereas shutting down leaves an unreadable encrypted disk. Pulling the drive or rebooting also locks the volume.
h: Encrypted and running? The key is in RAM, so don't turn it off.

q: A junior examiner at a regional police lab has a seized laptop drive in an evidence bag. She plans to attach the original drive to her workstation and browse it in a forensic suite to look for deleted files, because 'the tool is read-only anyway.' Her supervisor stops her. What is the BEST practice?
o: Analyze a verified bit-for-bit image, not the original
Analyze the original directly, since read-only tools can't change it
Copy the user's documents folder to a USB drive and analyze that
Analyze the original but record a hash of each file opened
w: Examiners work from a hash-verified bit-for-bit image so the original stays untouched and admissible. Mounting the original risks changes and challenges in court, a file copy misses deleted data and metadata, and hashing files you open doesn't protect the original.
h: Preserve the original; analyze the copy.

q: An analyst is building a timeline from the sources below and finds that the firewall shows the outbound connection two hours before the EDR records the process that made it. What should the analyst do FIRST?
c:
EDR (workstation)    local time UTC-5   14:05:12  powershell.exe -> 45.95.11.8:443
Firewall             UTC                19:05:13  ALLOW 10.2.4.77 -> 45.95.11.8:443
Proxy                UTC-7              12:05:14  CONNECT 45.95.11.8:443
o: Normalize every source to UTC before correlating
Trust the firewall timestamp and discard the EDR events
Assume the EDR agent's clock was tampered with by malware
Correlate the events by their order of arrival in the SIEM
w: Each source logs in a different time zone; converted to UTC they line up within two seconds. Discarding data, assuming tampering, or relying on arrival order all produce a wrong timeline.
h: Before you compare clocks, put them in the same time zone.

ack: Options restate the three alerts named in the stem.
q: A SOC receives three alerts in an hour: a malware detection quarantined on one laptop, a confirmed domain admin login from an unknown country, and a phishing email reported by a user before clicking. Using a severity-based triage model, which should be handled FIRST?
o: The domain admin login from the unknown country
The quarantined malware detection on the single laptop
The phishing email the user reported before clicking it
Whichever alert arrived first in the SIEM queue that hour
w: A privileged account possibly in an attacker's hands has the greatest potential impact, so it comes first. The malware was already quarantined and the phish wasn't clicked, and first-in-first-out ignores severity.
h: Triage by impact, not by arrival.

q: Before imaging a seized drive, a forensic technician connects it to the workstation through a hardware device that passes read commands but blocks any write commands. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this device?
o: To ensure the evidence isn't modified during acquisition
To speed up imaging for very large drives at the lab
To decrypt drives protected with full-disk encryption
To record who handled the drive for the chain of custody
w: A write blocker prevents the examiner's system from altering the evidence while it is read. It doesn't speed imaging, decrypt drives, or replace chain-of-custody documentation.
h: Read everything; write nothing.

q: A SOC confirms that a workstation is beaconing to a command server and that the user's credentials were used on two other hosts. Which TWO actions belong to the containment phase?
o: Isolate the workstation from the network with EDR
Block the C2 domain and IP at the egress firewall
Reimage the workstation from the gold image
Restore the user's files from last night's backup
Hold the lessons learned meeting with stakeholders
w: Containment limits spread and cuts the attacker's control: isolating the host and blocking the C2 destination. Reimaging is eradication and recovery, restoring files is recovery, and lessons learned comes last.
h: Contain = stop the spread and cut the line.

q: Rules are processed top-down and stop at the first match. What happens to SMTP from 198.51.100.9 to 10.1.5.25 on TCP 25?
c:
1  DENY    TCP  198.51.100.0/24  any            any
2  PERMIT  TCP  any              10.1.5.25      25
3  PERMIT  TCP  any              10.1.5.0/24    443
4  DENY    IP   any              any            any (log)
o: Denied by rule 1
Allowed by rule 2
Allowed by rule 3
Denied by rule 4
w: 198.51.100.9 is inside 198.51.100.0/24, so rule 1 matches first and denies it; rule 2 never gets a chance. Rule 3 is for 443, and rule 4 is never reached.
h: The first rule that names you decides.

q: A branch router uses the stateless ACL below on its WAN interface (inbound). Branch users can send web requests, but pages never load. What is the BEST fix?
c:
ip access-list extended WAN-IN
 10 permit tcp any host 192.0.2.10 eq 443
 20 deny   ip any any log
o: Permit established return traffic (TCP ACK) to the inside network
Move rule 20 above rule 10 so denied traffic is logged first
Change rule 10 to permit UDP instead of TCP on port 443
Remove the log keyword from rule 20 to reduce router CPU load
w: A stateless ACL doesn't track sessions, so replies to users' outbound requests (sources on port 443, destined to ephemeral ports) hit the deny; allowing established traffic or the ephemeral return range fixes it. Reordering would block everything, UDP isn't the issue, and logging doesn't drop packets.
h: Stateless rules forget you asked; let the answers back in.

q: Malware on a law firm's workstation reached its command server over TCP 8443 without any alert. The firewall's only outbound rule is 'PERMIT IP 10.0.0.0/8 any any.' Users need web browsing through the proxy, DNS through internal resolvers, and nothing else. Which change BEST fixes this?
o: Default-deny egress except from the approved forwarding hosts
Add a deny rule for TCP 8443 above the existing permit rule
Enable logging on the existing permit-all outbound rule
Block the command server's IP address at the firewall only
w: Default-deny egress that allows only the proxy and DNS servers to reach the internet closes every unapproved channel, not just this one. Blocking one port or one IP is whack-a-mole, and logging a permit-all rule still allows the traffic.
h: Outbound should be a short list, not 'anything goes.'

q: An auditor flags the rule below on a hospital's internal firewall. The radiology viewing servers need only HTTPS from the radiology workstation subnet 10.40.8.0/24. Which revised rule BEST applies least privilege?
o: PERMIT IP 10.40.8.0/24 to 10.50.2.0/24 on any port
DENY IP 10.40.0.0/16 to 10.50.2.0/24 on any port
w: Least privilege narrows both the source (the radiology subnet) and the service (HTTPS). The other permits leave either every port or the whole /16 open, and a blanket deny breaks the clinical workflow.
h: Narrow the who and the what.

q: An HVAC vendor needs SSH to one controller (10.70.1.15) during a maintenance window every second Tuesday from 09:00 to 11:00, from the vendor's office at 198.51.100.40. Which rule BEST meets this?
o: A time-limited SSH rule from 198.51.100.40 to 10.70.1.15
Permit SSH from any source to 10.70.1.15 at all times with logging enabled
Permit all traffic from 198.51.100.40 to the 10.70.1.0/24 subnet
Permit SSH from 198.51.100.40 to 10.70.1.15 at all times of day
w: A time-based rule limited to the vendor's source, the single host, and SSH opens access only when it's needed. Any-source access, subnet-wide access, and always-on access each leave far more exposed than necessary.
h: Right source, right host, right port, right time.

q: A firewall audit asks which rules below can NEVER match any traffic because earlier rules always catch it first. Which TWO rules are shadowed?
o: Rule 2
Rule 4
Rule 3
Rule 5
Rule 1
w: Rule 1 already permits every source to 10.9.0.0/16 on 443, so rule 2's deny for 10.9.4.10:443 never matches. Rule 3 permits all of 10.1.0.0/16 on 22, so rule 4's deny for 10.1.7.7 never matches. Rules 3 and 5 match their own traffic, and rule 1 is first.
h: A narrow rule below a broad one that already covers it never runs.

q: A global bank has grown to 4,800 RBAC roles because access depends on combinations of job, region, business line, and data sensitivity, for example 'Teller-Ohio-Retail-PII'. Role reviews take months. Which model would MOST reduce this complexity?
o: Attribute-based access control with central policies
Discretionary access control so each data owner shares as they see fit
Mandatory access control with security labels on every customer record
Rule-based access control limited to time-of-day restrictions
w: ABAC evaluates attributes (job, region, line of business, sensitivity) in a few policies instead of encoding every combination as a role. DAC decentralizes and loses consistency, MAC is rigid and label-driven, and time-of-day rules don't address the combinations.
h: When roles multiply from combinations, switch to attributes.

q: An audit at a fintech finds that a senior developer can write code, approve her own pull request, and deploy it to production without anyone else involved. Which control BEST addresses this finding?
o: Separation of duties: a second person must sign off on each merge
Least privilege: remove her access to the source code repository
Job rotation: move her to a different team every six months
Mandatory vacation: require two weeks of consecutive time off each year
w: Requiring a different person to approve changes before production splits the critical task. Removing repository access stops her from working, and job rotation and mandatory vacation detect fraud over time rather than preventing self-approval.
h: No one should approve their own work into production.

q: An access review shows that 2,300 employees can open the Payroll folder, because a parent folder was shared with 'Everyone' years ago and the Payroll folder inherits that permission. HR is the only group that should have access. What is the BEST fix?
o: Break inheritance on Payroll and grant HR only
Remove 'Everyone' from the whole file server at the root level today
Ask each of the 2,300 employees to stop opening the Payroll folder
Encrypt the Payroll folder so only the file server can read it
w: Stopping inheritance on the sensitive folder and granting only the HR group fixes its access without guessing at the impact elsewhere. Changing the root at once could break many shares, asking users isn't a control, and server-side encryption doesn't stop authorized-looking access through the share.
h: Sensitive folders shouldn't inherit 'Everyone.'

q: If the identity provider fails, a hospital's IT staff need a way into critical systems, but routine admin work must always go through the PAM platform. Which approach BEST meets both needs?
o: Sealed, monitored break-glass accounts tested regularly
A shared admin password taped inside the data center's network rack
Permanent local admin rights for every member of the IT team
Disabling MFA on all admin accounts so logins still work in an outage
w: Break-glass accounts with vaulted or sealed credentials, alerting on any use, and regular testing provide emergency access without weakening everyday controls. Taped passwords, standing admin rights, and disabling MFA all weaken security permanently.
h: Emergency access: sealed, alarmed, and tested.

q: At a research lab, scientists who own data sets routinely share them with outside collaborators by adding personal email accounts to folder permissions, and nobody can track who has access. Which change BEST addresses the root problem?
o: Role-based groups with owner-approved, time-limited sharing
Let each scientist continue sharing but email IT a monthly list
Mandatory access control labels on every lab data set and user
Full-disk encryption on every researcher's workstation
w: Discretionary sharing by individual owners caused untracked access; centrally managed groups with approved, expiring external access restore control and visibility. Self-reported lists aren't reliable, MAC is heavy-handed for research collaboration, and disk encryption doesn't govern sharing.
h: When everyone shares their own way, no one knows who has what.

q: Regulators require a brokerage to show that privileged access to trading systems is still appropriate. Admin rights currently change monthly and are reviewed once a year. Which practice BEST satisfies the requirement?
o: Quarterly attestation of privileged access by system owners
Annual reviews of all access, privileged or not, by the internal audit team
Permanent admin rights granted to traders so reviews aren't needed
A once-only review after each new privileged account is created
w: Regular attestation, more frequent for privileged access and done by the people accountable for the systems, gives regulators evidence that access stays appropriate. Annual reviews lag monthly changes, permanent rights make it worse, and a one-time check misses later drift.
h: High privilege, high frequency of review.

q: A retailer uses SSO for 40 SaaS apps, but accounts inside each app are still created and removed by hand, and former employees keep app accounts for weeks. Which capability BEST closes this gap?
o: Automated provisioning from the identity provider via SCIM
Longer password requirements for each SaaS application's local accounts
A quarterly reminder asking app owners to delete inactive accounts
Turning on MFA inside each SaaS application's own login page
w: SCIM lets the identity provider create, update, and deactivate app accounts automatically when HR changes occur, closing the deprovisioning gap. Password rules and MFA protect logins but don't remove accounts, and reminders are slow and unreliable.
h: SSO controls the login; SCIM controls the account.

q: A healthcare startup is building a native mobile app and wants patients to sign in with an existing identity provider and get an ID token describing the user, plus an access token for its API. Which standard BEST fits?
o: OpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2.0
SAML 2.0 browser POST profile assertions
LDAP simple binds from the mobile app to the directory
Kerberos tickets issued directly to the patients' phones
w: OIDC adds an identity layer (ID tokens) to OAuth 2.0 access tokens and is designed for modern web and mobile apps. SAML is browser-centric and awkward on native apps, direct LDAP binds expose credentials and the directory, and Kerberos isn't built for internet-facing mobile clients.
h: OAuth grants access; OIDC tells you who's there.

q: At 00:00 on the first of the month, every employee at a company suddenly failed to sign in to a SaaS app that uses SAML SSO. The SaaS app's logs show the error below. What is the MOST likely cause?
c:
SAML Response rejected: Signature validation failed.
Expected signing certificate thumbprint: 7A:19:...:C4 (expired 2026-10-31)
Received signing certificate thumbprint: 2F:8B:...:91
o: The IdP moved to a new certificate the app doesn't yet trust
Every user's password expired on the first of the month at midnight
The SaaS app's TLS certificate expired and browsers refused to connect
The users' MFA tokens drifted out of sync with the identity provider
w: The IdP is now signing with a new certificate while the service provider still expects the expired one, so every assertion fails; updating the SP's metadata or certificate fixes it. Password expiry or MFA drift wouldn't fail everyone at once with a signature error, and a TLS failure would block the connection before any SAML processing.
h: When the IdP changes its signature, the SP must learn the new one.

q: An investigation shows an attacker used the SQL service account's password to log on interactively to a file server over RDP. The account only needs to run the SQL service on two database servers. Which change BEST reduces this risk?
o: A managed service account with interactive logon denied
A longer password for the service account rotated every year
Adding the service account to the Domain Admins group for monitoring
Enabling SMS-based MFA for the service account's interactive logins
w: Denying interactive and RDP logon and using a group managed service account with automatically rotated passwords keeps the account to its purpose. A longer, yearly password still allows misuse, Domain Admins makes it worse, and SMS MFA doesn't fit non-interactive service accounts.
h: Service accounts run services; they don't sit at desks.

q: A nurse transferred from oncology to the emergency department six months ago. She still has full access to the oncology scheduling and chemotherapy ordering systems. Which identity lifecycle process failed?
o: The mover process that removes access when roles change
The joiner process that grants new employees initial access
The leaver process that disables accounts at termination
The identity proofing process performed during onboarding
w: When someone changes roles, their old access should be removed as new access is granted; skipping that causes privilege creep. Joiner covers new hires, leaver covers departures, and identity proofing happens at onboarding.
h: Movers should lose the old keys when they get the new ones.

q: An audit finds 60 accounts in the company's project management SaaS that log in with local passwords instead of SSO, including several belonging to people who left the company months ago. Which control BEST prevents this from recurring?
o: SSO-only enforcement plus SCIM deprovisioning
A stronger password policy for the app's local accounts
Monthly manual exports of the app's user list for review
Disabling the app's audit log to reduce clutter for admins
w: Requiring SSO means no one can log in outside the identity provider, and SCIM removes accounts automatically when people leave. Stronger local passwords and manual exports still leave local accounts alive, and disabling logging hides the problem.
h: If you can log in around SSO, you can stay after you leave.

q: A bank's PAM vault holds the domain admin password, which admins check out for emergencies. An auditor notes that the same password stays valid after each checkout, so anyone who saw it could reuse it later. Which PAM setting addresses this?
o: Automatic password rotation after each check-in
Longer checkout windows so admins don't need to request access again
Emailing the password to each admin so the vault isn't a bottleneck
Allowing multiple admins to check out the same password at once
w: Rotating the credential after every use means a seen or copied password is useless later. Longer windows, emailing passwords, and concurrent checkouts all increase exposure and weaken accountability.
h: Once used, change it.

q: Several employees clicked a link that asked them to grant an app named 'DocuSign Secure Viewer' permission to read their mailbox and files. No password was entered, yet attackers then read their mail through the app's API. Which control BEST prevents this?
o: Allow only admin-approved or verified apps to receive user consent
A longer password policy for all employee mailbox accounts
Blocking access to the real DocuSign website from company networks
Requiring employees to change their passwords every 30 days
w: Malicious OAuth apps abuse user consent rather than passwords, so restricting consent to verified publishers or admin-approved apps stops the grant. Password policies are irrelevant when no password is stolen, and blocking the real vendor doesn't stop a fake app.
h: No password stolen? Check what apps were given permission.

q: After an audit, a credit union is rewriting its password policy, which currently requires eight complex characters changed every 60 days. Help desk data shows most resets come from forced changes, and users often write passwords down. Which policy BEST reflects current NIST guidance?
o: Long passphrases checked against breached lists, with no forced periodic change
Eight characters with mandatory symbols and forced changes every 60 days
Twelve characters with a required number and a monthly expiration date
Complexity rules enforced by a client-side script on the login page
w: Current guidance favors length, screening against known-compromised passwords, and changing passwords only when compromise is suspected. Short complex passwords and frequent forced changes lead to predictable patterns, and client-side enforcement can be bypassed.
h: Long and not leaked beats short and complicated.

q: A biometric scanner on a data center door occasionally admits the wrong person. The security director wants to make false admissions much rarer, accepting that legitimate staff may sometimes need a second scan. Which adjustment does this describe?
o: Lower the FAR, accepting a higher FRR
Lower the false rejection rate, accepting a higher false acceptance rate
Set the device exactly at its crossover error rate and leave it there
Replace the biometric reader with a PIN keypad for every employee
w: Tightening the threshold reduces false acceptances (FAR) at the cost of more false rejections (FRR), the trade-off the director accepts. The reverse loosens security, the CER is just the point where the rates meet, and a keypad removes the biometric factor entirely.
h: Fewer impostors in means more insiders scanning twice.

q: A company's authenticator app shows a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds and works without a network connection, because the phone and server share a secret and both know the current time. What type of one-time password is this?
o: TOTP
HOTP
SMS OTP
Static PIN
w: Time-based one-time passwords derive each code from a shared secret and the current time window. HOTP uses an event counter instead of time, SMS codes are sent over the network, and a static PIN never changes.
h: T for time, H for hits on the counter.

q: Federal contractors at an agency badge into buildings and log in to workstations with a PIV card that holds a certificate and requires a PIN at the reader. Which factors does this combination use?
o: Something you have and something you know
Something you are and something you know, through the card's chip
Two instances of something you have, the card and its certificate
Somewhere you are and something you have, through the badge reader
w: The card (and the certificate on it) is something you have, and the PIN is something you know, which makes it multifactor. No biometric is involved, the card and its certificate are one possession factor, and the reader location isn't an authentication factor here.
h: Card plus PIN: have plus know.

q: A network team managing 300 routers and switches wants AAA that encrypts the entire session payload, uses TCP, and can authorize each individual command an admin runs. Which protocol BEST fits?
o: TACACS+
RADIUS
LDAP
SAML
w: TACACS+ encrypts the whole body, runs over TCP, and separates authorization so it can be done per command, which suits device administration. RADIUS encrypts only the password and is aimed at network access, LDAP is a directory protocol, and SAML is for web SSO.
h: TACACS+ for Typing commands on network gear.

q: A company wants sign-ins from a managed laptop on the corporate network to need only a passkey, while sign-ins from a new device or an unusual country trigger extra verification or are blocked, without asking every user for more prompts every time. Which approach BEST fits?
o: Risk-based conditional access
Requiring three authentication factors for every sign-in, every time
Blocking all sign-ins from outside the corporate network completely
Shorter password lifetimes for users who travel frequently for work
