w: Context-aware (risk-based) authentication raises requirements only when signals look risky, keeping normal logins simple. Always demanding three factors adds friction everywhere, blocking all off-network sign-ins stops remote work, and password lifetimes don't respond to context.
h: Ask for more proof only when something looks off.

q: A help desk lead is building a short security awareness quiz for new branch staff, because several of them recently described a PIN as a second factor. Which TWO items are 'something you have'?
o: A hardware OTP token
A smart card
A memorized PIN
A fingerprint scan
GPS location
w: Physical objects you possess, such as tokens and smart cards, are 'something you have.' A PIN is something you know, a fingerprint is something you are, and location is somewhere you are.
h: If you can lose it in a parking lot, it's something you have.

q: After a firewall firmware upgrade, a SIEM's 'blocked outbound to known-bad IP' rule hasn't fired in two weeks, although raw firewall logs still arrive. A spot check shows the destination IP field in parsed events is empty. What is the MOST likely issue?
o: The new log format broke the SIEM's parser
Attackers stopped contacting known-bad IP addresses after the upgrade
The firewall stopped sending logs to the SIEM after the upgrade
The SIEM's license expired and it now ignores new correlation rules
w: Raw logs arrive but key fields come out empty, which points to the parser not matching the new format; detections that depend on that field quietly stop. The logs are arriving, a sudden change in attacker behavior is unlikely, and a license issue wouldn't empty one field.
h: Logs in but fields empty? Fix the parser.

q: During a past incident, an attacker with domain admin rights deleted the SIEM's local copies of authentication logs to hide activity. The CISO wants logs that can't be altered or deleted, even by administrators, for one year. Which control BEST meets this?
o: Forwarding logs to immutable (WORM) storage
Restricting the SIEM console to members of the Domain Admins group
Compressing the logs nightly to save storage space on the SIEM
Increasing the SIEM's local disk size so logs are never rotated out
w: Write-once storage with retention locks stops even privileged users from altering or deleting logs during the retention period. Restricting the console to Domain Admins gives the attacker's level of access the keys, and compression or larger disks don't prevent deletion.
h: Logs an admin can delete are logs an attacker can delete.

q: A company moved its file storage and identity to a cloud provider last year. During an incident, analysts found no record of who had changed bucket permissions or created API keys, because the SIEM only collects on-premises logs. What should be added?
o: Collect the provider's control-plane audit logs centrally
More NetFlow collectors on the on-premises core switches
Endpoint DLP agents on every employee's laptop and desktop
A full packet capture appliance at the on-premises internet edge
w: Control-plane actions such as permission changes and key creation are recorded only in the provider's audit and identity logs, so those must be collected. On-premises NetFlow, endpoint DLP, and edge packet capture never see API calls made in the cloud.
h: If it happened in the cloud console, the evidence is in the cloud's logs.

q: An analyst needs to determine exactly which files and commands an attacker sent over an unencrypted protocol during a 20-minute window yesterday. Flow records show the connection but not its content. Which data source would provide this?
o: A full packet capture covering that window
NetFlow records from the core switch for the same period
SNMP traps from the network devices during the window
The vulnerability scanner's report from the previous week
w: Only packet capture records full payloads, so it can show the actual files and commands. NetFlow summarizes connections without content, SNMP traps report device events, and scan reports show weaknesses.
h: To see what was said, you need the recording, not the call log.

q: Responders at a university can't tell which process on Windows lab machines made suspicious outbound connections, because default Windows logging doesn't record process command lines or network connections per process. Which addition would MOST improve this visibility at low cost?
o: Deploying Sysmon with a tuned configuration
A larger Windows Security event log size on each lab machine
Disabling Windows Firewall logging to reduce noise in the SIEM
Weekly vulnerability scans of every lab machine in the university
w: Sysmon records process creation with command lines and the network connections each process makes, filling exactly this gap. A bigger log holds more of the same events, turning off firewall logging removes data, and vulnerability scans don't record activity.
h: Sysmon tells you who on the box made the call.

q: During an investigation, analysts find the edge firewall keeps only 24 hours of logs locally, and the suspicious activity happened four days ago. The firewall can send syslog. What is the BEST long-term fix?
o: Forward firewall logs to the SIEM and retain them by policy
Increase the firewall's local log buffer to hold a full week
Export the firewall's logs manually to a USB drive each morning
Turn on debug-level logging so the firewall records more detail
w: Centralizing logs with defined retention keeps them available for investigations regardless of the device's limits. A bigger buffer still has a ceiling, manual exports are unreliable, and debug logging fills the buffer faster.
h: Devices forget; the SIEM remembers.

q: A SOAR playbook automatically disabled the CEO's account in the middle of a board presentation after a false-positive impossible travel alert. Leadership wants to keep automation but avoid repeats for high-impact actions. Which change BEST fits?
o: Require analyst sign-off before disruptive steps on VIP accounts
Turn off the SOAR platform and handle every alert manually instead
Exclude all executives from every detection rule in the SIEM
Let the playbook disable accounts only on weekends and holidays
w: Keeping automation for enrichment and low-risk actions while requiring analyst approval for disruptive steps on critical accounts balances speed and safety. Dropping SOAR loses its benefits, exempting executives blinds the SOC to high-value targets, and limiting actions to weekends makes no sense.
h: Automate the routine; approve the drastic.

q: A regional distributor is deciding whether to buy a flood barrier system for its main warehouse. Using the figures below, what should the risk committee conclude on cost alone?
c:
Asset value (warehouse and stock):  $2,000,000
Exposure factor (flood):            25%
Annual rate of occurrence:          0.05  (once in 20 years)
Flood barrier system:               $40,000 per year, lowers ARO to 0.01
o: Decline it; it costs more than the $20,000 a year it saves
Buy it; it cuts the annualized loss expectancy by $500,000 a year
Buy it; any control that reduces ARO by 80% is always justified
Decline it; the single loss expectancy is only $25,000 per flood
w: SLE = $2,000,000 × 0.25 = $500,000. ALE drops from $25,000 (× 0.05) to $5,000 (× 0.01), a $20,000 annual saving, which is less than the $40,000 cost. $500,000 is the SLE, not the annual reduction, a percentage cut alone doesn't justify the spend, and $25,000 is the original ALE, not the SLE.
h: Compare what it saves per year with what it costs per year.

q: A hospital's qualitative risk assessment rates each risk on 1-5 scales. Leadership can fund one treatment this quarter. Using the excerpt below, which risk should be treated FIRST?
c:
Risk                                  Likelihood  Impact
R1 Ransomware via exposed RDP              4          5
R2 Lost unencrypted USB with PHI           3          4
R3 Website defacement                      4          2
R4 Data center flood                       1          5
o: R1, with the highest likelihood-times-impact score
R4, because its impact is rated as severe as any other risk
R3, because it is the most likely to happen this quarter
R2, because it involves regulated patient health information
w: R1 scores 20 (4 × 5), well above R2 (12), R3 (8), and R4 (5). R4 matches the top impact but is very unlikely, R3 is likely but low impact, and R2 involves PHI but still scores lower overall.
h: Likely and severe beats either one alone.

q: A credit union's board approves two statements for its cyber program. The first says, 'We accept moderate risk to grow digital banking.' The second says, 'No single cyber event may cause more than $500,000 in losses or more than four hours of online banking downtime.' Which term BEST describes the second statement?
o: Risk tolerance
Risk appetite
Residual risk
Inherent risk
w: Tolerance sets the specific, measurable limits around the appetite; the first statement is the appetite itself. Residual and inherent risk describe risk levels after and before controls, not limits.
h: Appetite is the attitude; tolerance is the number.

q: A risk register lists 'Payroll vendor outage delays employee pay' and assigns it to the IT security manager. The auditor says the owner is wrong. Who should own this risk?
o: The HR or payroll leader accountable for that process
The IT security manager, since security staff maintain the register
The payroll vendor's account manager named in the contract
The external auditor who reviews the register every year
w: Risk owners are the business leaders accountable for the process the risk affects, here payroll. Security maintains the register and advises, vendors can't own your risk, and auditors must stay independent.
h: Whoever loses sleep if the process fails owns the risk.

q: After buying a $5 million cyber insurance policy, a retailer's CFO says the breach risk has been 'fully transferred.' A board member disagrees. Which point BEST supports the board member?
o: Insurance moves some financial loss, not reputational harm or legal duties
Insurance policies always exclude ransomware and other cyber events
Transferring risk only works for physical assets such as buildings
A $5 million policy is too small to count as any risk transfer at all
w: Insurance offsets covered costs, but the company still suffers reputational harm and remains responsible for compliance, notification, and customers. Cyber policies cover many cyber events, transfer applies to more than physical assets, and partial coverage is still transfer, just not complete.
h: You can insure the bill, not the blame.

q: A business impact analysis finds that an online pharmacy's ordering system can be down for at most six hours before patients are harmed and regulators intervene. The IT team proposes an RTO of eight hours because restores take that long today. What is the problem with the proposal?
o: The RTO exceeds the maximum tolerable downtime
The RTO should equal the recovery point objective exactly
An RTO can never be shorter than the current restore time
The maximum tolerable downtime should be raised to match the RTO
w: The RTO must fit inside the maximum tolerable downtime, so recovery capability has to improve to meet six hours or less. RTO and RPO measure different things, objectives drive capability rather than the reverse, and MTD comes from business impact, not from IT's current speed.
h: The RTO must finish before the MTD runs out.

q: A bank's annual risk assessment ran in March. In July, it acquires a smaller bank with different core systems, and integration begins next month. What type of risk assessment should be performed now?
o: An ad hoc assessment focused on the acquired systems
None until the next scheduled annual assessment in March
A continuous assessment run by the vulnerability scanner only
A one-time assessment of last year's results, repeated unchanged
w: A major change outside the normal cycle calls for an ad hoc assessment focused on the new risks. Waiting until March leaves integration unassessed, a scanner covers only technical vulnerabilities, and reusing last year's results ignores the change.
h: Big change, unscheduled assessment.

q: A laptop worth $1,800 that holds encrypted customer files is lost. The company estimates each loss costs the device plus $600 in staff time, and no breach costs apply because of encryption. Losses occur about 15 times a year. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
w: SLE = $1,800 + $600 = $2,400, and ALE = $2,400 × 15 = $36,000. $27,000 counts only the device cost, $2,400 is the SLE, and $9,000 counts only staff time.
h: Add up one loss, then multiply by how often it happens.

q: A KRI for 'percentage of critical vendors without a current SOC 2 report' rose from 8% to 31% over two quarters, passing the register's 20% threshold, but nobody acted. Which risk management element failed?
o: Escalation to the owner when a KRI crosses its trigger
Choosing a qualitative rather than quantitative assessment method
Calculating the annualized loss expectancy for every vendor
Assigning a risk appetite to each individual vendor in the program
w: KRIs and thresholds exist to trigger action; the failure was that crossing 20% didn't trigger escalation to the risk owner. The assessment method, ALE math, and per-vendor appetite statements wouldn't have made anyone act.
h: A tripwire nobody watches isn't a tripwire.

q: Three critical vulnerabilities reached production last year because teams released code without security testing. The CISO wants a document that requires security activities at each stage from design to release. Which document type BEST fits?
o: A secure SDLC policy
An acceptable use policy for developers
A business continuity policy for development
A guideline suggesting optional code reviews
w: An SDLC policy sets mandatory security requirements across the development life cycle. An AUP governs acceptable use of resources, business continuity covers operations during disruption, and a guideline would be optional.
h: Security in every phase of building software.

q: An IT manager writes step-by-step instructions for removing a departing employee's access: disable the account, revoke tokens, transfer mailbox ownership, collect hardware, and confirm in the ticket. Which document type is this?
o: A procedure
A policy
A standard
A guideline
w: Ordered, step-by-step instructions for performing a task are a procedure (here, offboarding). A policy states intent, a standard sets mandatory specifics, and a guideline recommends.
h: Numbered steps = procedure.

q: A company reviews its information security policy every October. In March, a new state privacy law takes effect that changes breach notification deadlines. What should happen with the policy?
o: An out-of-cycle review to reflect the new law
Nothing until the regular October review cycle comes around
The legal team rewrites only the incident response procedure
A memo to employees replaces the policy's notification section
w: Policies need monitoring and revision when external requirements change, not just on a calendar. Waiting leaves the policy non-compliant for months, changing only the procedure leaves the policy contradicting it, and a memo isn't a governed policy change.
h: New law, new review, whatever the calendar says.

q: Employees at a law firm label documents inconsistently, and some confidential client files have been sent to outside parties unencrypted. Which document would MOST directly fix the root problem?
o: A data classification policy with handling rules
A password standard requiring longer passphrases for every user
An acceptable use policy covering personal web browsing at work
A change management procedure for document management releases
w: A classification policy defines the labels and how each level must be handled, including encryption for external sharing. Password rules, browsing rules, and release procedures don't address labeling or handling.
h: Name the levels, then say how each is handled.

q: A security team is splitting a long policy into a policy and supporting standards. Which TWO statements belong in a standard rather than the policy?
o: Laptops must use AES-256 full-disk encryption with TPM 2.0
Administrator accounts must authenticate with FIDO2 security keys
The company is committed to protecting customer information
Management will support information security across the organization
Employees should consider locking their screens when stepping away
w: Standards specify mandatory technical requirements, such as named algorithms and authentication methods. Commitment and support statements are policy intent, and 'should consider' is guideline language.
h: If it names the technology, it's a standard.

q: A business unit wants to keep running an unsupported HR application for another year because replacement is costly. Security has documented the risks and compensating controls. Who should formally accept this risk?
o: The executive accountable for that application
The security analyst who documented the risks and controls
The help desk team that supports the application's users
The application vendor that no longer supports the product
w: Risk acceptance belongs to the business owner accountable for the system and its outcomes. Security advises and documents, the help desk supports users, and a vendor that has ended support can't accept your risk.
h: Whoever owns the outcome signs the acceptance.

q: A retailer in good standing with PCI DSS asks whether PCI is a law that the government could fine them under. Which statement is MOST accurate?
o: It's an industry standard enforced by card brands through contracts
It's a federal law enforced by the U.S. Department of Commerce
It's an international treaty that applies to every online retailer
It's a voluntary guideline with no penalties for non-compliance
w: PCI DSS is an industry standard that the card brands enforce through merchant and acquirer agreements, with fines and loss of processing as consequences. It isn't a statute or treaty, and it carries real contractual penalties.
h: PCI comes from the card brands, not the legislature.

q: A U.S. e-commerce startup with no offices in Europe begins selling to customers in Germany and France and tracking their behavior on its site. Its counsel says GDPR now applies. Which governance consideration does this illustrate?
o: Global regulations that apply beyond a country's borders
Local regulations that apply only within one city's limits
Industry standards enforced only through card brand contracts
Internal policies that the startup's board chose to adopt
w: GDPR applies to organizations anywhere that offer goods or services to, or monitor, people in the EU, so it is a global external consideration. It isn't a local ordinance, an industry standard, or a voluntary internal policy.
h: Serve EU residents, follow EU rules, wherever you sit.

q: A manufacturer's security priorities keep clashing with operations because each department sets its own goals. The CEO wants a forum where leaders from IT, operations, legal, HR, and finance agree on security priorities and resources each quarter. Which governance structure fits?
o: A cross-functional security steering committee
A security operations center staffed around the clock
An outsourced managed detection and response provider
The change advisory board that approves IT changes
w: A steering committee of business leaders sets direction and priorities across departments. A SOC and MDR provider run day-to-day detection, and a CAB approves individual changes rather than setting strategy.
h: Priorities are set by leaders together, not by the people on shift.

q: A company's policies say they are reviewed annually, but an audit finds most haven't been touched in four years and several reference systems that were retired. Which governance activity is MOST clearly missing?
o: Monitoring and revision of policies on their stated schedule
Initial creation of policies for each new system
Annual security awareness training for all staff
Penetration testing of the policy management tool
w: Governance includes monitoring policies and revising them as required; skipping that leaves outdated rules. The policies exist, training communicates them, and a pen test of a tool doesn't keep content current.
h: A policy nobody revises slowly stops describing reality.

q: At a regional bank, the CISO reports to the CIO. Twice, the CIO deferred security fixes to meet IT project deadlines, and the board heard about the risks only afterward. Which change BEST addresses this structural issue?
o: Give the CISO an independent line to the CEO or a risk committee
Have the CISO report to the head of IT operations instead of the CIO
Merge the CISO and CIO roles so one person balances both priorities
Have the CISO report only to the external auditors each year
w: An independent reporting line lets security risk reach decision-makers without being filtered by the function it oversees. Reporting deeper into IT or merging roles worsens the conflict, and external auditors must remain independent of management.
h: Security shouldn't report only to the team it checks.

q: A hospital system's CISO and CRO have drafted a cyber risk appetite statement that will guide budget, vendor, and project decisions in every hospital in the system. The CEO asks which body must give final approval for it to carry that authority. Which body should approve it?
o: The board of directors
The SOC's shift supervisors
The IT help desk manager
The external penetration testers
w: Risk appetite is a top-level governance decision approved by the board. SOC staff, help desk managers, and outside testers carry out or assess work; they don't set organizational appetite.
h: Appetite comes from the top.

q: A state banking regulator issues binding cybersecurity rules that all chartered banks must follow, and it examines banks for compliance. In governance terms, what is the regulator?
o: A government body with enforcement authority
An internal committee of the banks' boards
A voluntary industry information sharing group
A third-party vendor selling compliance software
w: Regulators are government entities that set and enforce external requirements on the organizations they oversee. They aren't internal committees, voluntary ISACs, or vendors.
h: Regulators are government, and their rules aren't optional.

q: A credit union's core banking vendor has strong controls, but it stores backups with a smaller cloud provider that the credit union has never reviewed, and that provider just had a breach. Which risk did the credit union's vendor program MOST likely overlook?
o: Fourth-party risk from the vendor's own subcontractors and providers
Concentration risk from using too many vendors in total
Inherent risk from the core vendor's application code
Internal risk from the credit union's own employees
w: Vendors' subcontractors (fourth parties) can expose your data, so supply chain analysis and contract terms must reach them. The issue isn't too many vendors, the core vendor's code, or internal staff.
h: Your vendor's vendor holds your data too.

q: A vendor's SOC 2 Type II report covers January 1 through June 30. It's now November, and the next report won't be issued until February. During due diligence, what should the customer request to cover the gap?
o: A bridge letter from the vendor covering July to now
A brand new SOC 2 Type II report issued within the week
The auditor's internal working papers from the last audit
A copy of the vendor's cyber insurance policy declarations
w: A bridge letter, the vendor's attestation that controls haven't materially changed since the report period, covers the gap until the next report. A full Type II can't be produced in a week, auditors' working papers aren't shared, and insurance doesn't describe controls.
h: A bridge letter spans the gap between reports.

q: A health system is ending its contract with a transcription vendor that held patient recordings and had VPN access. Which set of actions BEST completes offboarding?
o: Cut all connectivity, retrieve the data, and get a destruction certificate
Send a thank-you letter and leave the VPN account active just in case
Ask the vendor to keep the recordings until the next audit is done
Delete the vendor from the vendor list and rely on the contract's end date
w: Offboarding must close every access path, recover or confirm destruction of the data, and document it. Leaving accounts active, letting the vendor keep data, or just removing it from a list leaves exposure behind.
h: Close the doors, collect the data, and get it in writing.

q: A hospital's third-party risk team is reviewing a payroll vendor. The vendor's questionnaire says all admin access uses MFA. The independent penetration test summary the vendor supplied lists the finding 'admin portal accessible with password only.' The contract is due to be signed next week. What should the team do NEXT?
o: Request evidence and remediation for the discrepancy
Accept the questionnaire, since vendors know their own systems best
Accept the pen test and terminate the vendor contract immediately
Score the vendor using the questionnaire average and revisit at renewal
w: When self-reported answers conflict with independent evidence, the team should verify with evidence and track remediation. Trusting either source blindly or ignoring both doesn't resolve the risk.
h: When the story and the evidence disagree, ask for proof.

q: A logistics company's ERP, email, identity, backups, and SOC monitoring all come from one provider. That provider just had a 14-hour global outage, and every function failed at once. Which risk does this illustrate?
o: Vendor concentration risk
Data sovereignty risk from storing data in a foreign region
Insider risk from the provider's own administrative staff
Shadow IT risk from unsanctioned cloud application use
w: Relying on one provider for many critical functions creates a single point of failure. The outage wasn't about data location, a malicious insider, or unsanctioned apps.
h: All eggs in one vendor's basket.

q: A retailer is negotiating with a SaaS vendor that will hold customer data. Which TWO contract clauses MOST directly protect the retailer if the vendor is breached?
o: Breach notification within a defined number of hours
Indemnification for costs caused by the vendor's breach
A marketing clause allowing the vendor to list the retailer as a customer
A clause fixing the subscription price for three years
A clause requiring quarterly business review meetings
w: Fast breach notification lets the retailer meet its own obligations, and indemnification shifts costs the vendor causes back to the vendor. Marketing rights, price locks, and business reviews don't protect against a breach.
h: Tell us fast, and pay for what you caused.

q: Before a potential acquirer can review a startup's architecture diagrams and security assessments during due diligence, the startup wants a binding promise that the information won't be disclosed or used for anything else. Which agreement fits?
o: A non-disclosure agreement
A master service agreement
A service-level agreement
A memorandum of understanding
w: An NDA legally binds the recipient to keep shared information confidential and use it only for the stated purpose. An MSA sets terms for ongoing services, an SLA defines service levels, and an MOU is usually non-binding.
h: Sharing secrets before a deal? NDA first.

q: A managed hosting SLA promises 99.9% monthly availability, and credits apply if it's missed. In a 30-day month, the service was down for a single 50-minute outage. Was the SLA met?
o: No; 99.9% allows only about 43 minutes in 30 days
Yes; 99.9% allows about 72 minutes of downtime in 30 days
Yes; a single outage never counts against monthly availability
No; 99.9% allows no unplanned downtime at all during the month
w: 30 days is 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is about 43 minutes, so 50 minutes breaches the SLA. 72 minutes corresponds to 99.83%, single outages do count, and 99.9% does allow some downtime.
h: Three nines in a month is about 43 minutes.

q: Two state agencies agree to share an incident response team. They sign a formal document that spells out each agency's responsibilities, points of contact, and how data will be handled. No money changes hands, and it is more specific than a simple statement of intent. Which agreement type BEST fits?
o: A memorandum of agreement (MOA)
A statement of work (SOW)
A business partners agreement (BPA)
A non-disclosure agreement (NDA)
w: An MOA formally documents the responsibilities each party agrees to, with more detail and commitment than an MOU. A SOW defines paid project deliverables, a BPA governs a business partnership, and an NDA covers only confidentiality.
h: MOU = we intend to. MOA = here's who does what.

q: A company hires a managed SOC. It wants the contract to guarantee that critical alerts are triaged within 15 minutes and escalated to its on-call manager within 30, with credits if those times are missed. Where should these commitments live?
o: In the service-level agreement
In a memorandum of understanding
In the non-disclosure agreement
In the acceptable use policy
w: Measurable performance commitments with remedies belong in the SLA. An MOU isn't binding, an NDA covers confidentiality, and an AUP governs users' own conduct.
h: Numbers, deadlines, and credits: SLA.

q: Each quarter, a bank's compliance team presents the status of regulatory findings, overdue remediations, and policy exceptions to the board's risk committee. Which type of compliance reporting is this?
o: Internal reporting
External reporting
Regulatory examination
Independent attestation
w: Reporting compliance status to the organization's own leadership is internal reporting. External reporting goes to regulators or outside parties, an examination is performed by the regulator, and an attestation is a formal statement often given to outsiders.
h: Reporting up inside the house is internal.

q: After repeated failures to meet state cybersecurity requirements, a money transmitter is told by its regulator that it may no longer operate in the state. Which consequence of non-compliance is this?
o: Loss of license
Contractual impacts
Reputational damage
Financial fines
w: The regulator is revoking the company's authorization to operate, which is loss of license. Contractual impacts arise from customer or partner agreements, reputational damage is public perception, and fines are monetary penalties.
h: No license, no business.

q: A regulation requires the CEO and CISO of an insurer to sign an annual statement to the state regulator certifying that the cybersecurity program complies with its requirements. What is this signed statement?
o: An attestation
A self-assessment
A gap analysis
A risk register
w: An attestation is a formal declaration by responsible people that requirements are met, with personal accountability. A self-assessment is the evaluation work behind it, a gap analysis finds shortfalls, and a risk register tracks risks.
h: Signing your name that it's true = attestation.

q: A national retailer complies with federal breach notification rules, which allow 60 days. One state where it operates requires notifying residents within 30 days. A breach affects customers in that state. What should the retailer do?
o: Notify affected people in that state within 30 days
Notify within 60 days, because federal rules always take priority
Notify only when the federal deadline passes, to keep it consistent
Skip state notification because the company is national, not local
w: When local or regional laws are stricter, the organization must meet the stricter requirement for affected residents. Federal law doesn't automatically override stricter state notification laws, and operating nationally doesn't exempt a company from state law.
h: Follow the strictest rule that applies to the people affected.

q: A company passed its PCI DSS assessment in March. In May, attackers stole card data using a technique that the assessment didn't test. The CEO asks how they could be breached while compliant. Which explanation is MOST accurate?
o: Compliance is a baseline at a point in time, not security
The assessor must have made an error, because compliant firms can't be breached
PCI DSS covers only physical security, so it ignored the attack
Compliance automatically expires 60 days after the assessment
w: Compliance shows minimum requirements were met when assessed; threats and environments change, so security has to go beyond the checklist and be continuous. Compliant organizations can be breached, PCI covers far more than physical controls, and compliance doesn't expire after 60 days.
h: Compliant on audit day isn't the same as secure every day.

q: An external auditor asks a SaaS company to show that quarterly access reviews happened throughout the past year. The team performed the reviews but discussed them in meetings and kept no records. What is the MOST likely audit outcome?
o: A finding, because there's no evidence the control operated
No finding, because the team says it performed the reviews
A finding only if a breach occurred during the year being audited
No finding, because access reviews aren't auditable controls
w: Auditors test evidence; a control without records is treated as not performed. Verbal assurance isn't evidence, findings don't depend on a breach, and access reviews are commonly tested controls.
h: If it isn't documented, it didn't happen, as far as an audit is concerned.

q: An online merchant fails its annual PCI DSS assessment. Its acquiring bank sets a 90-day remediation deadline, which the merchant misses because the fixes were never funded. Which TWO consequences are MOST likely?
o: Fines passed on through its payment processor
Losing the ability to accept card payments
Revocation of its business incorporation by the state
Criminal charges against every employee
Automatic loss of its domain name registration
w: Card brands fine acquirers, who pass the fines to merchants, and persistent non-compliance can end card processing under the merchant agreement. State incorporation, criminal charges against all staff, and domain registration aren't PCI consequences.
h: PCI penalties come through the payment chain.

q: A regulator requires an insurer to keep evidence of security control operation for five years. The GRC team currently stores screenshots on individual laptops, and several were lost when staff left. Which change BEST supports compliance?
o: A central evidence repository with retention controls
Asking each employee to back up their screenshots monthly
Recreating missing evidence when the auditor asks for it
Shortening the retention period in the insurer's own policy
w: A central, access-controlled repository with retention settings keeps evidence available and trustworthy for the required period. Personal backups are unreliable, recreating evidence is falsification, and an internal policy can't override the regulator.
h: Evidence belongs in the vault, not on someone's laptop.

q: A European customer emails a retailer asking for all the personal data it holds about her. The retailer keeps her data in its CRM, order system, marketing platform, and support tickets. Which response BEST satisfies the access request?
o: Copies of her data across all systems, with purposes, recipients, and retention
Only the account profile page she can already see when logged in
A summary of the retailer's privacy policy and cookie notice
Her order history, since that's the only data she created herself
w: An access request covers personal data held about her wherever it's stored, plus information such as purposes, recipients, and retention. A profile page, a policy summary, or order history alone is incomplete.
h: Access means everything you hold about me, and why.

q: A gaming company collects each player's full date of birth, home address, and phone number at signup, but only needs to confirm players are over 16. Which privacy principle is it MOST clearly violating?
o: Data minimization
Data sovereignty
Data retention
Data custodianship
w: Collecting more personal data than the purpose needs violates data minimization; an age confirmation would do. Sovereignty is about location and jurisdiction, retention about how long data is kept, and custodianship about technical care.
h: Collect only what you need for the purpose.

q: A customer's valid erasure request is processed in all production systems, but her records remain in immutable 90-day backups that can't be edited. What is the BEST approach?
o: Let backups age out on schedule, and suppress her data if any backup is restored
Delete the entire backup set immediately to remove her records
Refuse the request because backups contain her personal data
Edit the immutable backups by disabling their retention locks
w: When deletion from backups isn't feasible, organizations document it, let the backups expire on schedule, and make sure the data is removed again if a backup is ever restored. Destroying all backups harms resilience, refusing outright ignores the valid request, and breaking immutability undermines ransomware protection.
h: Can't edit the backup? Make sure she doesn't come back with a restore.

q: A European clinic is engaging a cloud transcription provider that will process patient data on the clinic's instructions. Under GDPR, which document must govern how the provider handles that data?
o: A data processing agreement between controller and processor
A memorandum of understanding signed by the clinic's director
An acceptable use policy that the provider's staff acknowledge
A service-level agreement covering transcription turnaround
w: GDPR requires a contract between controller and processor that sets out processing instructions, security, sub-processors, and data return or deletion. An MOU isn't binding, an AUP covers user conduct, and an SLA covers performance rather than data protection.
h: Controller to processor: put the instructions in a DPA.

q: A company's retention policy deletes customer support emails after two years. Legal counsel has issued a legal hold for emails related to a pending lawsuit, some of which are 23 months old. What should happen next month when they reach two years?
o: Keep them; the hold suspends scheduled deletion
Delete them on schedule, because the retention policy came first
Delete half of them and keep the rest as a compromise
Ask the support agents whether they still need the emails
w: A legal hold suspends normal deletion for the covered data until counsel releases it; deleting held data risks sanctions for spoliation. Retention schedules yield to holds, compromises aren't allowed, and support agents don't decide legal preservation.
h: A legal hold freezes the clock.

q: At a university, the registrar owns student records. A separate person maintains the data dictionary, resolves duplicate student entries, and makes sure fields are used consistently across systems, but doesn't run backups or servers. Which role is this?
o: Data steward
Data custodian
Data controller
Data subject
w: A data steward manages data quality, definitions, and consistent use on behalf of the owner. A custodian handles technical care such as storage and backups, the controller is the organization deciding purposes, and subjects are the students.
h: Stewards keep the data clean and consistent.

q: A German subsidiary needs to send employee records to its U.S. parent's HR system. Counsel says a valid legal mechanism is required for this transfer. Which option is MOST appropriate?
o: Standard contractual clauses or an adequacy framework
Encrypting the records and relying on that alone
Getting a verbal OK from each employee's manager
Storing the records in a U.S. region without any agreement
w: Cross-border transfers of EU personal data need an approved mechanism, such as adequacy (for example, a certified framework) or standard contractual clauses. Encryption is a safeguard but not a legal basis, manager approval isn't valid, and simply storing data in the U.S. is the problem itself.
h: Data leaving the EU needs a legal passport.

q: During an authorized test of a bank's online banking platform, a tester discovers credentials for the bank's payment switch, a system explicitly listed as out of scope. What should the tester do?
o: Stop, avoid using them, and report it to the contact
Use the credentials to show impact, since the finding is critical
Keep testing quietly and include the switch in the final report
Post a sanitized write-up publicly to warn other banks
w: The rules of engagement define authorized scope; touching an out-of-scope system is unauthorized, so the tester stops and reports through the agreed contact. Using the credentials, continuing quietly, or publishing breaks the engagement and possibly the law.
h: Out of scope means hands off, then phone home.

q: A physical penetration tester is caught after hours in a client's data center by police called by a guard. The tester can avoid arrest by showing which document?
o: A signed authorization letter from client leadership
The tester's company business card and LinkedIn profile
A copy of the vulnerability scan report from last month
The client's public website listing its office address
w: Physical testers carry a signed authorization (often called a 'get out of jail' letter) naming the scope and an emergency contact who can confirm it. Business cards, scan reports, and public addresses prove nothing about authorization.
h: Carry the signed permission slip.

q: A tester compromises a web server in a hospital's DMZ, then uses it as a foothold to reach and test an internal database server that can't be reached from the internet. What is this technique called?
o: Pivoting
Passive reconnaissance
Persistence
Privilege escalation
w: Using a compromised host to reach other systems is pivoting (lateral movement). Passive reconnaissance gathers information without touching the target, persistence keeps access over time, and privilege escalation raises rights on a system.
h: Pivot: stand on one box to reach the next.

q: A SaaS company runs annual penetration tests each January. In June it launches a new public API and migrates authentication to a new identity provider. When should the next penetration test happen?
o: After these major changes, before the next annual test
Next January, as the annual schedule already plans
Only after a breach shows that the changes were risky
Never for the API, since APIs aren't tested by pen testers
w: Significant changes such as new public interfaces and authentication redesigns warrant testing when they happen, not just on the calendar. Waiting until January leaves months of exposure, waiting for a breach is too late, and APIs are a common pen test target.
h: Test when it changes, not just when the calendar says.

q: A company plans to penetration test applications it runs in a public IaaS cloud. Before testing begins, what should it confirm about the cloud provider?
o: That the provider's policy permits the planned activities
That the provider will run the whole test for free
That the provider's own data centers are within scope
That the provider has turned off its DDoS protection
w: Cloud providers publish rules on what customers may test on their own resources, and some activities need notice or are forbidden. Providers don't run your test, their own infrastructure isn't yours to test, and disabling provider protections isn't something to request.
h: In someone else's cloud, check their rules before you test.
